Link copied <p> Australia has introduced new mandatory climate reporting rules that require business owners to estimate their company 's emissions and outline plans to tackle future risks . <p> The legislation , passed in 2024 , is the most significant change to reporting requirements and director responsibilities in a generation , according to the Australian Institute of Company Directors ( AICD ) . <p> It will require companies to disclose their greenhouse gas emissions and explain how a range of future climate scenarios could impact their business , in a sustainability report filed alongside their financial data . <p> Initially , the legislation will apply only to Australia 's largest companies but by 2027 , thousands of corporate and not-for-profit organisations will be included -- something AICD managing director and CEO Mark Rigotti @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ approach their mandatory disclosures . <p> " It 's actually quite a fundamental step change in reporting and there probably has n't been as significant a change since 2003 , when we moved from sort of domestic financial standards to international financial reporting standards , " Mr Rigotti said . <h> What 's changing ? <p> The law requires companies to publish an annual " climate statement " that outlines any material climate risks they may face , and their scope one , two and three greenhouse gas emissions . <p> Information about any of the company 's strategies , governance or risk management plans pertaining to those risks and emissions must also be disclosed . <p> And it will have to run those risks through a range of scenarios , which at minimum must include a global temperature increase of 2 degrees Celsius and a global temperature increase of 1.5C . <h> What are ' scopes ' ? <p> Scope 1 : " Direct emissions " generated within and by the company , by its operations . <p> Scope 3 : Broader emissions generated in a company 's supply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sustainability reporting has been done on a voluntary basis and under a range of differing standards , according to Julia Bilyanska , partner in charge of climate change and sustainability at KPMG . <p> Now , they 'll be formalised under standards set by the International Sustainability Standards Board ( ISSB ) , and require auditing like the rest of the organisation 's financial statements . <p> Once the sole domain of sustainability departments , companies are restructuring to adapt to the new regime . <p> Company directors could face legal action if they fail to produce credible emissions forecasts , under draft laws proposed by the federal government . <p> " Of course , by 2050 there are some uncertainties , but as long as there 's transparency and disclosure , I think that 's where the board 's focus should really be , " Ms Bilyanska said . <p> " Our focus will be , as auditors of this information , is to make sure that there is a really good transparent presentation of how the business is being managed . " <h> Early mover <p> The legislation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aligned mandatory standards about how climate change may impact the financial future of corporations . <p> The European Union leads the pack , with its Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requiring corporations to report on a broad range of sustainability-related matters . <p> But with the ISSB standards being formalised only recently , Canada , New Zealand , Japan and Brazil are among other countries where elements of the standards are being incorporated into corporate reporting requirements . <p> " The European legislation in particular is already penetrating globally because a lot of the value chains are located in South America and China , " Ms Bilyanska said . <p> The new laws mark a generational shift in the type of information Australian companies will be legally required to disclose . In the 1980s excess cases of leukaemia and lymphoma were noticed around the Sellafield nuclear plant in England . <p> A UK government investigation unexpectedly found that the risks for leukaemia and lymphoma were higher than in the surrounding population . In 2007 , the US Department of Energy examined all the reliable data available worldwide , confirming a significant increase in leukaemia for children living near nuclear power plants . <p> The clearest findings on this subject come from a large national German study from 2008 . It examined leukaemia among children living near any of Germany 's 16 operating nuclear plants over a 25-year period . <p> It showed that the risk of leukaemia more than doubled for children living within 5 kilometres of a nuclear plant . Nuclear proponents quote a UN study with an 80-kilometre radius showing no harm , but the much larger distance dilutes any problems for those living much closer . <p> Opposition Leader Peter Dutton . Thyroid cancer increased by 17 per cent and leukemia by 9 per cent . <p> For workers in the nuclear industries , there is also clear evidence of increased risk of death from cancer . Indeed , recent findings show even some non-cancer diseases are increased , such as heart attack and stroke . <p> The best evidence for this comes from INWORKS , a multi-country study of over 300,000 radiation industry workers observed for more than 30 years . Their radiation exposures and health outcomes were carefully monitored and compared with the general population . <p> The cancers caused by radiation blend in with other cancers - they are not like the characteristic mesothelioma caused by asbestos . @@119563409 <h> Trading on weather takes off in unpredictable climate <h> By Lou Del Bello <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> As the world 's climate becomes increasingly volatile , businesses that depend on predictable weather are turning to financial products that compensate them when there 's a heat wave , a drought or an unusually persistent bout of rain . <p> Unlike better-known catastrophe bonds , which help to shield insurers against rare natural disasters , so-called weather derivatives offer protection from less severe but more common meteorological events . These contracts help companies to manage risks that may go barely noticed , such as a warmer winter or a rainier summer . <p> Storm clouds seen from WilliamstownCredit : Jason South <p> Traditionally , companies involved in agriculture , hydropower and tourism tended to buy insurance against rarer types of disruptive weather events , such as cyclones . Those policies will only pay out if it can be proved that their finances had been materially affected . <p> Buyers of weather derivatives @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ weather deviate from an agreed norm . A solar power plant operator could get paid when there 's an unusually high number of cloudy days . A farmer could get a payout if unseasonably hot weather wilts their crops . <p> Many businesses that purchase weather derivatives use them to stabilise revenue streams that would otherwise be more erratic due to fluctuating weather . <p> Loading <p> Some contracts focused on temperature are listed on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange ( CME ) . Using so-called heating degree days ( HDD ) and cooling degree days ( CDD ) as parameters , they pay out when temperatures deviate from daily averages against an 18C baseline . Other indexes simply calculate the contract 's value by adding up the daily average temperatures through the contract period . <p> The highest volume of weather derivative contracts is currently traded " over the counter " -- that is , off the public markets . This is because buyers often prefer to work directly with sellers to customise the contracts so they include several payout triggers . <p> For example , a gas distribution company @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lead a consumer to use less gas . <p> Advertisement <p> An energy retailer may want to hedge the risk of lost revenue if summer turns out to be cooler than normal . These variables can be plotted with precision using models that combine historical data with short and long-term weather predictions to create a product suited to the client . <p> Demand for weather derivatives is soaring , with average trading volumes for listed products jumping more than 260 per cent in 2023 , according to the CME Group . The number of listed weather derivative contracts that year was 48 per cent higher than the previous May . <p> Those publicly traded derivatives may represent just 10 per cent of all activity . According to some industry estimates , there may be as much as $US25 billion ( $40.2 billion ) of weather derivatives overall . <p> Weather derivatives started trading over the counter in 1997 and evolved into an investment class listed on the CME , initially in the US alone and later in Europe and Australia . In 2004 , the CME expanded its portfolio to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ markets . <p> They took off more recently as weather became more unpredictable and businesses were forced to find new ways to track related risks . Part of the impulse for this has come from their own investors , who leaned on companies to disclose their climate-related risk exposure and make plans to address it . <p> A growing body of literature suggests the impacts of climate change on the global economy may be much greater than previously thought . A study found that a 1 ? C rise in temperature may lead to a permanent decline in global economic output of as much as 12 per cent , a situation comparable to the 1929 Great Depression . <p> Loading <p> Erratic weather is already changing energy demand patterns around the world , increasing the appetite for financial instruments designed to offset that risk . According to one United Nations study , the cities of Toronto and Vancouver may see a reduction in annual energy demand in their office buildings of as much as 10 per cent between 2056 and 2075 . In Sweden , heating demand is forecast to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is also playing a part : Satellites and other weather monitoring technologies are providing big data sets to track the most complex , localised weather patterns , allowing the finance industry to design derivative products that are tailored to each buyer 's situation . <p> Weather derivatives first emerged in the US and are now expanding rapidly across the developed world , especially in energy and agriculture . Other industries are also getting involved . For example , the New York City Metropolitan Transportation Authority has reportedly used them to hedge the risk of colder winters that could disrupt mass transit services . <p> Yet , they 've not yet taken off in developing countries that still rely heavily on agriculture and therefore have potentially the most to gain . <p> India is making some initial moves . The government recently made it possible to trade the weather , a first step toward the creation of home-grown weather derivatives . But there 's scant awareness of the products among local businesses , and a mass of red tape required to get involved . <p> Various studies have highlighted the potential @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ countries too , but beyond a few limited experiments the market remains underdeveloped .

This is because commercial nuclear power plants produce plutonium as a by-product of operation , and historically this plutonium has been used to make nuclear bombs . <p> There are two alternative essential ingredients in the making of nuclear weapons . The first is an isotope of uranium , U235 , which is fissionable , and the second is plutonium U239 , also fissionable . The first occurs in nature , but needs to be refined from the ore : just under 1 per cent of naturally occurring uranium ore is U235 , and nearly all the rest U238 . <p> A complex process is needed to produce weapons-grade ( 90 per cent ) U235 for bombs . The alternative active ingredient , plutonium , is a man-made element initially created in plants dedicated to making it , though now it can be supplied from commercial nuclear power plants . <p> In the normal functioning of the nuclear plant , neutrons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some are absorbed by the neighbouring U238 atoms . The plutonium is made when neutrons enter the U238 isotope , transforming the atom into U239 , plutonium . Energetic neutrons from the fission of the U235 atom itself may also enter U238 atoms , transforming them to plutonium . <p> It is hard to know whether the initial " atoms for peace " commercial nuclear power plants were used from the beginning to make plutonium for bombs . Certainly , at first , claims were made for nuclear power that the electricity produced would be ' too cheap to meter ' , though this claim may have been made out of ignorance , rather than as a deliberate deception . @@119755306 <p> A weekly rummage through essential cultural ingredients for a good life : design , architecture , food , travel , and fashion . <p> " Even the most ardent foodies and chefs ... they might have been to a farm , they might even have been to a slaughterhouse , but the chances they 've been to a refrigerated warehouse are really , really slim , " Nicola Twilley , author of Frostbite : How Refrigeration Changed Our Food , Our Planet and Ourselves , tells ABC Radio National 's Blueprint for Living . <p> " I do n't think you can understand what it is we eat and why until you understand refrigeration . " <p> And your home refrigerator is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the cold chain process , Twilley says . <p> So this summer , as you struggle to fit Christmas leftovers into the fridge , spare a thought for the complex chain of events that led to that food being in your fridge in the first place . <p> While researching for her book , Twilley spent time @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ temperature-controlled warehouse space . ( Supplied : Geoff Manaugh ) <p> The cold chain process refers to the series of refrigerated warehouses , shipping containers and entirely refrigerated ships that food passes through before it reaches consumers . <p> And while refrigeration is an aspect of life that we take for granted , Twilley says our ability to create artificial refrigeration is a relatively new phenomenon . <p> " We 've been making fires since before we were modern Homo sapiens . But creating cold is really recent -- and it 's not that people had not noticed ice is cold . ... What they had no clue about was how that cold existed . " <p> Yet refrigeration has changed the way our world works . And , because of its enormous impact on climate change , it will continue to reshape it . <h> Where did refrigeration start ? <p> While people have been preserving food with natural ice for thousands of years , the creation of artificial cold was a puzzle for many of the great pioneering scientists , including Galileo , Leonardo da Vinci and Robert @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ English philosopher and early science intellectual , died in 1629 trying to figure out how to artificially create cold . <p> " He was stuffing a chicken full of ice and caught a cold and died , " she says . <p> In the 19th and early 20th century , the first cold chain began as a global trade in natural ice . <p> " What happened was a high school dropout from Boston , Frederic Tudor ... harvested ice from lakes and then stored it in ice houses , and he worked out how to ship it around the world , including to Australia , " Twilley says . <p> This natural ice trade was a game changer . Ice was no longer purely a luxury item . Instead it began to revolutionise the meat , vegetable , fruit , dairy and fish industries . <p> Twilley says as the potential of this refrigeration process was slowly recognised , a number of engineers persisted in trying to create cold artificially . <p> James Harrison , a Scottish-Australian printer based in Geelong , was the first to build and sell @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's first commercial refrigeration machine was made for a London brewery . ( Supplied : Museums Victoria ) <p> " He had noticed when he was printing in the summer ... that the ink would smudge and when he would wipe the type with ether , it evaporated and that would cool the type . " <p> From observing this process of evaporation , Harrison had the idea of how to make ice , Twilley says . <p> Harrison 's first ice-making machine began operation in 1851 on the banks of the Barwon River in Geelong . <p> Then a few years later , Harrison created the first commercial ice-making machine for a brewery . <p> Given that it 's impossible to make lager without cold temperatures , brewers were some of the biggest consumers of ice , Twilley explains . <p> And so , we have " beer to thank for refrigeration " . <h> The fridge determines what we eat <p> Since then , the fridge has become a ubiquitous part of the food and beverage industries and our everyday life . <p> Twilley points out that the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that keep in cold storage . ( Getty : Karen Moskowitz ) <p> But some foods are resistant to refrigeration and instead demand freshness . Twilley says these foods have slowly disappeared from our diets . <p> " For example , the United States has a tropical fruit of its own called the paw paw and you never find that in the supermarket . The tropical fruit you find in the supermarket is the banana , because that 's the one that you can harvest while it 's green , refrigerate and then artificially ripen . You ca n't do that with the paw paw , and so it is not an instrument of commerce . " <p> So refrigeration has simultaneously increased what we can eat , as we can access food from anywhere in the world , but it also limits the fruit and vegetables varieties to those that keep well in cold storage . <h> How the cold chain process works <p> Both refrigeration and cold chain processes have become more sophisticated since the original ice-making machines and natural ice trade . <p> Now , individual food @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reach the consumer . <p> Most fruit and vegetables are placed in cold storage soon after being harvested . " <p> Specific food and drink have specialised refrigeration , she says . <p> " For example , orange juice and apple juice are stored in these gigantic tanks , eight storeys high , holding as much liquid as an Olympic-sized pool . @@119755826 <h> Save articles for later <p> A lethal combination of drought and powerful desert winds has fuelled the catastrophic mid-winter fires in Los Angeles in what should be the city 's rainy season . <p> Flames were being pushed by Santa Ana winds topping 97km/h in some places , and were expected to increase to 160km/h in mountains and foothills -- including in areas that have n't seen substantial rain in months . <p> The Santa Ana winds were behind most of southern California 's worst wildfires in history . They topple powerlines , rapidly turn a spark into an inferno , and they can make fires run downhill . <p> Former Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner Greg Mullins , who has spent years studying and fighting fires alongside Californian firefighters , said : " I 've fought fires during Santa Anas , and it 's scary because the fires run downhill just as fast as they do uphill . <p> " Those winds can be horrendous , and they are so dry that it does not matter if it is hot , you just get these incredible blast furnace @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are strong , gusty winds that bring hot , dry air from the desert to the Los Angeles basin . They are not unusual in autumn and winter , but they are usually far less intense . <p> They tend to coincide with the wettest season of the year . Los Angeles ' rainy season occurs from October to April , with most rain falling from December to February . This year , large parts of southern California , including most of Los Angeles , San Bernardino , Riverside , Orange and San Diego counties , are in drought . Los Angeles has not recorded rainfall over 2.54 millimetres -- the threshold that would reduce wildfire risk -- since last May . <p> Kent Porter , a photographer at The Press Democrat in Santa Rosa in northern California and who has been covering fires in the state for nearly 40 years , said the fire season had turned into an all-year phenomenon , especially in southern California . When he was in the Los Angeles area two weeks ago , he was shocked by how dry it was . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ since about July , " Porter said . " The drought is playing a big , big part in what is happening right now . " <p> The Santa Anas are caused by high pressure over the western deserts , and the sinking air becomes warmer and drier as it descends and flows towards southern California . <p> Between the desert and the Los Angeles basin are the San Bernardino Mountains , which top out at 3506 metres -- far taller than Australia 's largest mountain , Kosciuszko , at 2228 metres . <p> The air is funnelled into mountain passes and canyons that separate the desert from the city , becoming faster like a river that suddenly narrows and turns into rapids . <p> Other air hits the mountain peaks , and what little moisture remains in it forms clouds . This means that by the time the winds hit coastal areas , they are totally dry and often rapidly warming . <p> Usually , Los Angeles has cooler , more humid breezes from the Pacific Ocean . A Santa Ana wind can plunge humidity to the single digits @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and become more flammable . <p> Fires usually travel from the valley to the ridgeline , but the pressure of the winds coming over the mountains means the fires can rush downhill . <p> Mullins , the former Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner , is also a councillor with the Climate Council . He said the winter fires were occurring in an environment very similar to the east coast of Australia and the cause was clear . <p> " This is happening because of climate change , and it is what we predicted , " he said <p> " There is more energy in the environment because the atmosphere is hotter . Scientists will say they need to study the data , but I am saying this as a firefighter : this is unprecedented . @@119756403 <p> What are politicians to do ? They get panned for inaction on the cost of living , the housing crisis , weak productivity growth , climate change and inequality . <p> But they also get panned if they cut spending to ease inflation , do anything to reduce house prices , allow unproductive businesses to fail , introduce a price on carbon , or raise taxes to fight inequality . <p> Luckily , new research has found that politicians can have their cake and eat it too : they can implement economic reform and still get re-elected , provided they follow a few simple rules . <p> The research - by Alberto Alesina , Davide Furceri , Jonathan Ostry , Chris Papageorgiou and Dennis Quinn - did three very cool things . <p> First , they built the world 's most comprehensive dataset on economic reforms implemented in 90 countries over four decades . <p> Second , they constructed an equally huge dataset on every election that took place across roughly the same time period , including who won , who lost and by how much . <p> Third @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ impact economic reforms had on election outcomes and how this differed depending on the state of the economy ( while cleverly controlling for all the other things that impact election outcomes ) . <p> What are the lessons for whoever wins the next election in Australia ? <p> The first lesson is that voters punish governments for implementing economic reforms in the year before an election , but often reward governments for implementing reforms earlier in their term in office . <p> The reason is simple . Most economic reforms have winners and losers . <p> The pain felt by the losers tends to be immediate while the benefits felt by everyone else tends to take a while to have an effect . <p> The delayed gratification that comes from reform means that if governments implement these reforms close to an election , voters will see nothing but pain and will punish the government at the ballot box . <p> But if governments implement these reforms early , voters can only see the benefits by the time the next election rolls around . <p> The second lesson is that the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The researchers found that whether voters punished or rewarded governments for implementing reform depended largely on whether the economy was doing well or not . <p> Put simply , the researchers found that voters will punish governments if they implement reform when the economy is weak , but will reward governments that implement reform when the economy is booming . <p> This is a striking finding . It suggests that the old adage that " governments should never waste a good crisis " might not be correct . <p> It 's true that governments tend to implement more reforms during crises ( the researchers observed this in the data ) , but the governments that implement reforms during crises tend to get the boot afterwards . <p> Prime Minister Anthony Albanese . Picture by Keegan Carroll <p> The third and related lesson is that voters either do n't understand or do n't care about the time delay between when a reform is implemented and the impact of that reform on the economy . <p> If the economy is weak , voters will assume it was because your reform was bad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assume it was because your reform was great - even if it was the exact same reform . <p> In sum , the next government needs to be clever on timing . <p> The main advice is to go hard and go early . If the government is planning to commission a whole bunch of reviews that will take years to produce any recommendations , think again . By the time the reports and finished , consultations are complete , and legislation is before the Parliament , the next election will already be too close . <p> The better option is to run a new consultation process on old reports , of which there are plenty ( think : Henry Tax Review ) . This way , reforms can be implemented early in the parliamentary term and by the time the next election rolls around , the benefits will be flowing and voters will have forgotten about any earlier pain . <p> The government should also keep a close eye on the economy . If times are good , they can implement more reforms and do so closer to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ then implementing reforms as early as possible becomes even more important .

@@119796798 <h> Jacques Audiard 's Golden Globe-winning musical Emilia P ? rez is superficial , ham-fisted and fails to access the subversion made possible by camp . By Christos Tsiolkas . <h> Golden Globe-winning Emilia P ? rez fails in its attempt at relevance <p> Jacques Audiard 's new film , Emilia P ? rez , begins with an elating off-screen chorale , the music and the chanting recalling the classical ecclesiastic tradition . Puncturing the chorus , we hear market traders offering their wares . The camera descends across an urban nightscape in Mexico , isolating a woman working late in her apartment . The woman is Rita ( Zoe Salda ? a ) , a defence lawyer cynically preparing a brief for a man she knows is guilty of murdering his wife . She heads out to the street and we hear her resentful thoughts . The voiceover becomes song as she walks through the night markets . The crowds around her begin to accompany her in dance . <p> Unfortunately the lyrics and music of her song have none of the soaring majesty of the opening chorus . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lacking any sensuality or unity . That initial swooping pan from the celestial heavens to the mundane street life of the market encapsulates all that goes wrong with this film . <p> Emilia P ? rez wants to be a provocative and rousing mash-up of musical , telenovela , melodrama and socially conscious feminist film . Yet there is an underwhelming , pedestrian limitation to the screenplay and the music , and in Audiard 's direction . Most fatally , it is humourless . This week it won four Golden Globes , including the best picture awards for a musical or comedy and for non-English language . <p> Audiard is increasingly striving for the grand subject , which in effect is the straining for relevance ... In the end , Emilia literally becomes a saint . <p> The script , written by Audiard , is based on Boris Razon 's 2018 novel ? coute . Audiard initially adapted Razon 's book as a libretto for an opera , and I assume this inspired his desire to emphasise the melodramatic elements of the story . Soon after Rita has successfully prosecuted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of her ignoble client , she is kidnapped . Her capture has been organised by a major drug dealer , Juan " Manitas " Del Monte . Manitas makes Rita an offer . The narco wants to have gender-reassignment surgery , to live as a woman . If Rita helps make Manitas " disappear " and establishes a safe haven in Switzerland for his wife , Jessi ( Selena Gomez ) , and their two children , Rita will be financially set up for life . <p> Rita executes Manitas 's wishes , and soon she has established herself as a successful corporate lawyer in London . One night , at a high-end restaurant , she is seated next to another Spanish-speaking woman , Emilia P ? rez , who she quickly realises is her former kidnapper and benefactor . Emilia has one last task for Rita . She wants her wife and children back . <p> The best thing about the film is the performance of Karla Sof ? a Gasc ? n as Emilia . There are technical limitations to her acting , but she has a warm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ voice that she uses judiciously in delineating her portrayal of Manitas and then of Emilia . Her performance has a common thread of vulnerability that connects her past and present lives . <p> On screen , Gomez and Gasc ? n work well together and there are glimpses of affection and tenderness in the playing . However , Gomez 's role as Jessi is terribly undercooked in the writing , not much more than a soap-opera caricature of a narco wife . I wish the filmmakers had given more time to working through the relationship between the women and allowed us to comprehend the complications of betrayal experienced by Jessi . The revelation that Emilia is her former spouse occurs in the middle of a badly staged shootout , and so any emotional resonance from that realisation by Jessi is lost . <p> It 's hard to believe the screenplay is based on a novel and that Audiard has worked and reworked the material . It feels embryonic , very much a first draft . After transitioning , Emilia feels guilty for her past as a narco boss , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of drug cartels . The scene that gives rise to Emilia 's remorse is ludicrous and both the writing and performances lack credibility . <p> The questions of responsibility and guilt are never adequately addressed in this movie . We never understand , for example , why Rita is so forgiving about her abduction . Emilia and Rita dedicate themselves to their non-profit , but they seem to feel no shame or unease about continuing to live their haute-bourgeois lifestyles , presumably still benefiting from drug-trade money . The film 's nadir comes during a musical sequence set at a donor dinner . Rita attacks the assembled guests for covertly benefiting from cartel money . The lyrics are prissy , self-righteous platitudes , and the choreography is lazy , lifting from Bob Fosse but without any of that choreographer 's sensuality or verve . The filmmakers seem completely unaware that Rita is as hypocritical as the guests she is deriding . <p> It is not just this song . Throughout , the music is as ponderous as the script . Cl ? ment Ducol 's score is uninspiring , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The music does nothing to assist the film in developing either tension or narrative drive . I suspect Audiard and his editor , Juliette Welfling , must have realised the music was inadequate for their story during the assemblage of the film , and so it limps from one scene to the next without any cumulative emotional resonance . By the time we get to the irksome final act , the musical motifs have dropped away completely . <p> Audiard , Camille and Ducol are working in Spanish for the first time , which might explain some of the gawkiness of the dialogue and lyrics . I think the problem runs deeper than translation , however . The one effective musical moment , apart from the elegant opening , comes early in the film , in Tel Aviv , where Rita is engaged in a combative duet with an Israeli surgeon ( Mark Ivanir ) who will perform the gender-reassignment surgery on Emilia . The musical exchange is largely recitative , but the argument over the question of what is a soul has real urgency . Ivanir is commanding and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ actor in going toe to toe with him . It 's the one scene that does n't feel superficial or compromised in the execution . The scene reveals contradiction and complexity and for once there is a unity to the cinematic and musical language of the film . <p> Audiard is no stranger to complexity . His A Prophet ( 2009 ) is , I believe , the greatest French-language film of this century . In that film , he was unafraid of responding to the deep and disturbing questions of ethics and crime that are so superficially skimmed over in Emilia P ? rez . That complexity , and that intellectual and formal rigour , also were evident in A Self-Made Hero ( 1996 ) , The Beat That My Heart Skipped ( 2005 ) and Rust and Bone ( 2012 ) . They are all exceptional films , which makes the laziness of Emilia P ? rez even more shocking . <p> I got bored with the film early on , and to keep myself from dozing off I started to wonder what Pedro Almod ? var could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the intuitive understanding of the subterranean truths concealed within melodrama and camp that might have allowed the film and the performers to truly soar . Audiard does n't have a feel for the outlandish , for the way the almost heroic , subversive tendency of camp can undermine gender and sexual norms . When he attempts it , as in a musical number that takes place in a Bangkok hospital , the results are ham-fisted and embarrassingly unfunny . <p> The problem is n't that Audiard is n't queer , or that he is n't trans . I love his 1994 film See How They Fall , about a relationship between two men who exist on the fringes of the social order . It 's harsh and sensitive to how class complicates perceptions of queerness . Audiard 's great talent is to give us unflinching yet compassionate portraits of individuals . Even when working in the epic form , as he did with A Prophet , the scale of his story or his intentions never overwhelms his characters . We understand them intimately . <p> Audiard is increasingly striving for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for relevance . Are we prepared if something similar happens in a major city in Australia ? <h> READ MORE <h> Why is LA on fire ? <p> The areas north of LA have always been at high fire risk . The landscape was primed for fire , and then due to these winds , the fires grew extraordinarily fast . Fire suppression capacity was quickly overwhelmed . <p> In a place such as California , with its enviable aerial fire-fighting capacity , fires can usually be contained rapidly . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by these terrible winds . @@119800579 <p> The Commonwealth Bank ( CommBank ) has made a groundbreaking resolution to stop funding coal , oil and gas companies without genuine plans aligned with global climate goals . <p> Make no mistake , decisions like this from big banks are exactly what 's required to reduce risk from bushfires , floods and cyclones , fuelled by coal , oil and gas emissions . <p> The bank 's policy to this effect comes into force this week . But it 's hardly a happy new year for Australia 's biggest oil and gas companies like Santos and Woodside , which can no longer borrow money from Australia 's biggest bank to develop new gas fields , incompatible with internationally agreed global warming goals . <p> Suppose these fossil fuel companies want to pursue their gas expansion plans . In that case , they 'll have to do it without the backing of not only CommBank but a growing list of major international banks , which are closing their doors to fossil fuel producers undermining the transition to clean energy . Fascinating stuff for a statistics buff -- I ca n't get enough of it ! <p> Australia 's emissions in 2023 were about 450 million tonnes . <p> In 2024 , our emissions dropped 0.7% . That is the good news . <p> Buried in the report is a note that , for the last four years , the Climate Change Authority ( CCA ) has been recalibrating how much CO2 has been released or absorbed by the land and the forests . <p> This means the figures have been adjusted downwards by 4.3% due to recognising the hard work @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This means that the CO2 we pumped into the sky actually increased this year by 5% . That is the bad news ! <p> The Climate Change Authority found that our land and forests have been absorbing 4.3% more CO2 than we previously thought . This is a one-off anomaly . We wo n't be able to pull that stunt again . <p> So , how are we travelling overall ? <p> Well , way back in 2006 when we signed the Paris Climate Agreement -- brimming with hope and enthusiasm and pledging hand on heart , to reduce our emissions to zero by 2050 ( more or less ) -- our total emissions were 12% more than they are today , 18 years later . <p> We have 26 years left to reduce our emissions to zero by 2050 . <p> If we continue on our present trajectory we will reduce our emissions by a further 24% at best . 24 + 12 = 36% less than 2006 . <p> Still another 64% to go . Not good enough . Not even close . Dismal failure is staring us @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ federal government is confident that our efforts at reducing emissions are not following a straight trajectory , they like to think our production of renewable energy is increasing exponentially . <p> Alas , the statistics say otherwise . <p> As the graph below will show , every year our pathway to net zero becomes ever more precipitous . It is now dizzyingly vertiginous ! <p> We are fast approaching the point where achieving net zero by 2050 will require the complete cessation of all fossil fuel burning whatsoever ! <p> Despite our best efforts , we are falling behind . Why is that ? <p> The problem is glaringly obvious -- discretionary spending ! <p> According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics ( ABS ) -- my favourite bureau -- last year Australians spent fully 40% of their household budgets on discretionary items , things we do n't need -- and , that is in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis . <p> If we use our discretion , even briefly , we could reduce our emissions by a staggering 40% . <p> The climate crisis would be over and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about to happen , is it ? <p> We have come to expect our material wealth to increase steadily throughout our lifetimes -- culminating in an obscene amount of disposable income in our dotage . <p> We collectively refuse to give up one single morsel of that wealth in the name of solving the climate crisis or global inequality or anything else for that matter . <p> We have made it absolutely clear that our personal comfort and pleasure are far more important than anything else in the known universe -- and , any government foolish enough to challenge that attitude will be turfed out of office ! <p> So what on earth can we do about our predicament ? <p> Again the answer is obvious , but unpalatable . <p> If people refuse to reduce their discretionary spending for the sake of the climate , we must reduce discretionary spending by boycotting the economy . <p> Way back in World War II the economy was barely functioning , all resources and human power were put into the war effort . Food was rationed , and luxury items were not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ measures were called for , and drastic measures were implemented . It worked ! We won the war . <p> Back then people were prepared to make sacrifices because the bombs were falling all around them . Nothing like imminent death to wake you from your your slumber . <p> Whereas here in the present day , death is not imminent enough . All the death and destruction is taking place on the TV , in far-off lands , to people we do not care about . <p> By the time death arrives on our doorstep , it will , of course , be far too late . <p> We see smoke on the horizon and hope it will pass us by . It is only when we feel the heat on our cheeks that we leap into action and make a futile attempt at dousing the flames . <p> Ben Laycock lives in the bush in a small hamlet called Barkers Creek . He writes about almost everything , with a focus on climate change .

@@119828451 <h> Want some assistance ? <h> The Australian oil and gas sector understood the danger posed by fossil fuel combustion back in the ' 70s <p> In a new book , journalist Royce Kurmelovs look at the origins of the Australian petroleum industry , investigating what these companies knew about climate change when , and how they learnt to wield influence . <p> It was 1972 when the Australian oil and gas industry appears to have first publicly acknowledged the link between burning fossil fuels and the greenhouse effect . In this period those who gathered considered themselves " Men of Science " . They were skilled engineers and scientists who considered themselves equipped with the skills to tackle the world 's problems , so there was no fear in addressing the subject . <p> Against this backdrop , an internal tug of war was playing out within the industry at the time : " town gas " , made from coal , was being phased out and replaced by so-called " natural gas " , causing conflict between coal and gas producers . Australia ran on coal , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over suburban homes required a costly mass retrofit and education campaign . In this context , growing concerns about air pollution and the greenhouse effect benefited the gas producers , who argued that switching from coal to gas would buy the world more time to address the problem . <p> This appears to have annoyed those working for other fossil fuel producers , including R.S. Sherwin , a petroleum scientist with BP . At the 1972 APEA conference , Sherwin presented a paper titled , " Energy : Major Sources and Consumption " . His main focus was on quantifying the scale of demand for energy between 1972 and the year 2000 , but he also used the opportunity to take a swipe at colleagues in the gas industry concerned about air pollution , reminding them that burning gas still produced carbon dioxide . Sherwin specifically mentioned the greenhouse effect , noting it was first described by John Tyndall all the way back in 1861 , before emphasising a growing demand for fossil fuels . The situation needed to be watched carefully , he said . <p> " What is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ become damaging , " he warned , ominously , and then called into question the gas industry 's tactics : " Some gross oversimplifications and distortions of emphasis spring to mind . LNG is NOT a pollution-less fuel , since it produces carbon dioxide when burnt . " <p> Sherwin did not make explicit that he was referring to growing CO2 concentrations in the atmosphere caused by burning fossil fuels , but that is the clear implication . He similarly provided no data or referred to any resource to elaborate on his point . He simply accepted there was a relationship between burning fossil fuels and a changing atmosphere . <p> Then , having issued his rebuke , Sherwin moved on to other matters . <p> It was n't until the following year that a member of the industry went on record directly addressing the question , when a chemist with a special interest in human health , Hanns F. Hartmann , gave a paper at the 1973 APEA conference in Sydney . <p> Prior to World War II , Hanns Hartmann was a medical student at Vienna University in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Nazi Germany during the Anschluss . He was on holiday in Italy when his aunt telegrammed advising that , as an ethnic Jew , he should not come back . He fled , landing in the UK before heading for Australia , where he arrived in March 1939 at the age of 23 . Though he later trained as a chemist after xenophobic restrictions prevented him from re-enrolling in medicine on his arrival in Australia , Hartmann never lost his interest in the wellbeing of others . <p> The combination of his training in chemistry and lifelong interest in medicine resulted in an enduring professional focus on the effect of pollution on human health . At the time he addressed the APEA conference , Hartmann had been seconded as an officer of the Environmental Protection Council of Victoria ; he was also co-author of a recent book on ecology and a member of the Clean Air Society of Australia and New Zealand ( CASANZ ) . He had in fact organised the CASANZ conference in 1972 , just the year before , with the financial support of BP , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ BHP , Mobil Oil and Alcoa . The greenhouse effect had received top billing at this CASANZ meeting -- even as the issue was ignored by the oil and gas industry in their own forums . <p> There is no way to know how many people turned out for his presentation at the APEA National Conference in 1973 , but as the chief technical officer at the Australian Gas Association , Hartmann was n't exactly a headliner -- that honour was generally reserved for politicians and CEOs . Likewise , the title of his technical paper -- " The Role of Gas in Environmental Control " -- was n't particularly thrilling , and certainly did n't suggest what he was about to discuss . <p> With considerable brevity , Hartmann clearly outlined for his industry colleagues the consequences of burning fossil fuels , explaining that carbon dioxide 's atmospheric concentration had risen since the turn of the century from about 290 to 320 parts per million , and what that meant . <p> " Recent work indicates that perhaps one third of the carbon dioxide deriving from fuel combustion accumulates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) , while the remainder probably dissolves in the ocean , " he told them . " Great concern has been expressed over the so-called greenhouse effect , which could cause far-reaching climatic changes . Carbon dioxide , while transparent to shorter-wave solar radiation , absorbs longer-wave infrared radiation reflected into space from the earth 's surface and , therefore , acts like the glass roof of a greenhouse . " <p> With that , Hartmann had explained what the greenhouse effect was , how it worked , the role of the oceans as a carbon sink , the limits of knowledge at the time and the disconnect between what the empirical evidence appeared to show and what the theory of the greenhouse effect predicted should happen . He was , however , wrong about some specifics . Contrary to what Hartmann claimed , oceans and land-based ecosystems , when combined , absorbed roughly two-thirds of all CO2 . There were other technical errors , too , but it is unclear whether these were just poor writing , the work of an enthusiastic amateur or the product of a developing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of satellites . What is key , is that Hartmann clearly acknowledged the connection between burning fossil fuels and growing CO2 concentrations , and the potential for the resulting pollution to act like sleeping under a warm blanket in summer . <p> Hartmann concluded this section of his presentation with a qualification : although the consequences of this process " over the long-term " were then unknown , he said , " a close watch must be kept on long-term trends " . <p> At this point , the paper devolved into a discussion of the role car tailpipe emissions played in creating smog above Los Angeles , Sydney and Melbourne , leading into an argument in favour of gas as " practically free from air pollution if its combustion is properly regulated " . <p> It was , however , a remarkable summary that demonstrates the extent to which Hartmann was across the early research into the greenhouse effect . Not only was he able to put solid numbers to the problem , but he referred in his footnotes to industry documents published in journals and presented at symposiums @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Dallas , Texas , in 1968 , titled Global Effects of Environment Pollution . Edited by a young Fred Singer -- who would go on to become the godfather of climate denial after being denied a promotion while working for the US Environmental Protection Agency -- this tome contained early works by big names in climate science of the era . It also included a report by Robinson and Robbins , the same Stanford Research Institute scientists who had warned the American Petroleum Institute about the risk burning fossil fuels posed to the climate . <p> Though it is not a clear smoking gun -- Hartmann was not engaged in original research , and the papers he cited did not include the critical Robinson and Robbins report -- his work demonstrates that information was being shared between Australian industry figures and their counterparts overseas . Hartmann had delivered his paper at the APEA conference a full three years before the Australian Academy of Science would get around to publishing its own report on the issue , observing that human activities " could have an appreciable effect on the climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conference papers show the extent to which the Australian oil and gas industry already understood the danger posed by fossil fuel combustion at the dawn of the 1970s . Written by a petroleum scientist working for BP and the Australian Gas Association 's chief technical officer , they are clear evidence not only that the industry understood the link between burning fossil fuels and the greenhouse effect , but also that it was publicly discussing responses to the problem . <p> Others , however , were already pioneering an early form of climate denial . At the very same conference at which Hartmann spoke , a presentation by Sir Willis Connolly , former president of the World Energy Conference ( WEC ) , coolly dismissed carbon dioxide as a problem . <p> Connolly , who had been involved in setting up Victoria 's power grid and belonged to a brown-coal industry fraternity known as the " Barbarians " , reported that an internal committee within WEC had investigated pollution issues . This committee , he said , had not bothered to consider the risks posed by carbon dioxide -- " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was " not generally recognised as an air pollutant " . <p> When I showed all these documents to Dr Marc Hudson , an energy transitions scholar and climate historian from the University of Sussex , he was not surprised . By about 1969 , the potential risks of burning fossil fuels were understood . Out in the broader scientific community , work was already underway to pin down the specifics . The CSIRO had started to investigate the phenomenon , thanks to the foresight of a few particularly motivated scientists . Independent measurements of CO2 had first been recorded in Rutherglen , Victoria , in 1971 . APEA 's counterparts in the broader mining industry had also started to talk about the greenhouse effect , and the issue was even beginning to seep into public consciousness . Soylent Green screened in 1973 , the first film to depict a climate-shocked future . <p> What makes Hartmann and Sherwin 's presentations so important , Hudson said , is that they are a historical anchor point , pinpointing the moment at which global warming " pops up in the oil industry @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of awareness among the members of Australia 's oil and gas industry that there were risks associated with their commercial activities -- and of how little their talking points have changed over time . <p> " This is not five months ago , or five years ago , but more than five decades , " Hudson said . " One of the problems with thinking about climate policy is getting stuck in a perpetual present , too focused on the minutiae of who said what to whom at some recent roundtable or lobbying meeting . <p> " The next crucial step is knowing and being able to show how the oil and gas industry has been successfully influencing policy . @@119843104 <h> Term-limited and immune from accountability , Trump 's power is unprecedented <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Donald Trump enters office at the zenith of his power . His first year will be marked by the most extensive use of executive power under the Constitution in United States history . A political reality that normally applies to incoming presidents is not in play for Trump . Trump is now term-limited and does not have to face the voters again . Trump can exercise power to do what he wants and what he believes is right . At least until the midterm elections in 2026 , there is nothing the voters can do to curb his exercise of his power . <p> With Republican control of the House and Senate , there is virtually no likelihood Trump will be impeached or removed from office . @@119843533 <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> Californian climate scientists have published one of the timeliest findings in history . Hydroclimate whiplash -- a term for the phenomenon of savage seasonal swings between catastrophic rain and sapping drought -- is increasing , fast . <p> Driven by an atmosphere stoked hotter by the burning of fossil fuels , the whiplash is amplifying flash-floods , wildfires , landslides and disease outbreaks , the paper released overnight on Friday found . <p> A bicyclist stands among homes destroyed by the Palisades fire.Credit : AP <p> To illustrate this volatility , the authors zeroed in on California , where nine atmospheric river storms dumped record-breaking rain over a three-week period last ( northern hemisphere ) winter . Nearly 30 centimetres of rain hit the University of California , Los Angeles , which led the research , in two days last February . But this winter , barely a drop . <p> Weather whiplash has proliferated across the globe , including in Australia , which lurched from the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rain-making La Nina weather systems . <p> The scientists ' warning about the dangers of this whiplash is anything but academic . To the west of UCLA 's Romanesque campus halls , a catastrophic fire was incinerating thousands of homes in Pacific Palisades , unleashed by a 200 per cent burst of vegetation set off by last winter 's record rain and then sapped by unseasonal dryness . <p> To the east , the Eaton fire destroyed libraries , churches and street after street of houses . <p> The Palisades fire ravages a neighbourhood amid high winds.Credit : AP <p> " In that publication , fairly incredibly , we use the example of a transition from anomalously wet to anomalously dry conditions in California being an example of the tangible consequences of hydroclimate whiplash , " said Dr Daniel Swain , lead author of the Nature Reviewsarticle , on a livestream address . <p> " The consequences , from a wildfire perspective , are eerily , uncomfortably close to what has actually transpired this week . " <p> Advertisement <p> Hydroclimate whiplash is driven by the " expanding atmospheric sponge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ planet warms , the atmosphere can absorb 7 per cent more water . A wetter atmospheric sponge foists more intense , extreme bursts of rainfall , which produces huge fuel loads ready to combust when drought weather strikes . <p> Human-caused climate change has caused this whiplash to increase by 31 to 66 per cent globally . Rainfall volatility has accelerated , particularly in America , Europe and Australia , the authors wrote . <p> " The problem is that the sponge grows exponentially , like compound interest in a bank . The rate of expansion increases with each fraction of a degree of warming , " Swain said . <p> " The planet is warming at an essentially linear pace , but in the last five or 10 years there has been much discussion around accelerating climate impacts . This increase in hydroclimate whiplash , via the exponentially expanding atmospheric sponge , offers a potentially compelling explanation . " <p> The Climate Council tracked examples of whiplash in a report last year . A deadly blaze destroyed 32 homes during October 2023 in Queensland . @@119882959 <h> Cathy McGowan How community independent campaigns actually work <p> I 'm standing in Yulecart Memorial Hall on the Dartmoor-Hamilton Road , just west of Hamilton , Victoria . Together they sort out name tags , bring the makings of a delicious afternoon tea and chat with a sense of low-key excitement and expectation . <p> The occasion is an opportunity to meet the aspiring community independent candidate for Wannon , Alex Dyson . " <p> The community independents movement is motivated by a shared sense that our democracy is not delivering the benefits it could or should . The offer of this movement is for each and every one to be the change , to turn up , speak up and step up . <p> After introductions and a few short speeches , the work begins . Small groups practise the skills of actively listening , getting feedback on how to resist the temptation to interrupt and impose their own views . They learn how to engage . Thirty electorates have already identified community independent candidates and another 13 have begun processes for selecting theirs . Twelve are actively looking to 2028 . In every state and territory , tens of thousands of people are donating their time , resources and energy to practise democracy in this way . <p> The reason for this can be explained by a mix of push and pull . <p> The push is obvious . A deep sense of disillusionment and dissatisfaction with how politics is being done has impacted the major party vote , bringing it to historic lows . People are concerned about the failure of governments to meet basic needs . They are alarmed at the high levels of homelessness and the strains in public health and education . There is also -- always -- the failure to act effectively on the changing climate . <p> The pull is a community independence model based on hope and process . There is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ values and behaviours within and with community , there can be better outcomes . In Indi , where I was elected as an independent in 2013 , there has been significant improvement in the quality and level of representation and active engagement in politics . Locally there has been investment in infrastructure and improvement in the basic level of service delivery , especially in transport and telecommunications . <p> Community independents are popular , get re-elected and are having significant political impact . <p> There are many examples of legislation being introduced and amended by the community independents , with positive results . While ideas may be shared across groups , the processes within each electorate reflect local geography and the skills and experience of the leaders . <p> An active democracy is achieved not through telling or preaching . Operating somewhere in the murky intersection of classical and electronic music , his compositions are informed by his classical training and infused with the technical trickery of electronic music production . <p> Frahm -- who is heading to Australia next month for a national tour that kicks off at the Perth Festival in late February -- is one of the great shapeshifters of modern music . Google search his name and you 'll find countless articles hand-wringing over whether he 's a " classical " or " pop " artist . His agnostic approach , alternating between melancholic piano pieces and denser electronic-fused tunes , has won Frahm legions of fans from across the musical spectrum . <p> He 's been described by influential British critic Mary Anne Hobbs as " the single most important artist in the world " and lauded by one publication as having produced " one of the great musical contributions of the 21st century " . A recent article in The Guardian said Frahm was one of the main beneficiaries of a burgeoning interest in contemporary piano players , criticising the Spotify-powered rise to popularity of the likes of Frahm , Joep Beving and Ludovico Einaudi . <p> " I 'm not surprised that when certain things become hyped , that maybe the next step is that they become sour and damned , " Frahm says . " I feel like maybe whatever turned into being ' neoclassical ' or ' modern classical ' music is maybe just a little bit silly because , altogether , everything sounds a little bit like the same . I feel like maybe there is a redundancy in what is happening and maybe it 's time to move on . Barack Obama used his three-and-a-bit months to expand healthcare coverage to 11 million children , lift restrictions on funding of embryonic stem cell research and add 2 million acres ( 809,000 hectares ) to the national wilderness protection program . <p> Donald Trump , however , is not talking about 100 days . Rather , his focus is on " Day One " : what he plans to do immediately once he is inaugurated on January 20 . He has already half-joked that he 'll be a " dictator for a day " , that he 'll be " drill , drill , drilling " ( a reference to lifting environmental restraints and expanding oil and gas exploration ) and the speed of his reforms will be such that " your head will spin when you see what 's going to happen " . <p> He @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ border with Mexico , deport millions of undocumented migrants , wind back the Biden administration 's environmental programs , pardon rioters who stormed the Capitol in the 2021 insurrection and end the war in Ukraine ( if not on day one itself then , certainly , within 24 hours of intervening ) . " On day one of the Trump presidency , " he said at one campaign rally last year , " I 'm restoring the travel ban , suspending refugee admissions , and keeping terrorists the hell out of our country , like I had it before . " <p> So far , he 's made 41 promises for Day One action , by The Washington Post 's count ; US news site Axios says it 's closer to 100 . @@119918795 <p> The last 10 years have been the hottest on record . ( ABC News : Chris Lewis ) <p> **45;0;TOOLONG ... Link copied <p> It 's official -- 2024 was the hottest year on record and the first calendar year in which the earth was more than 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than pre-industrial times . <p> That 's a significant number , because it 's the target that world leaders agreed to under the landmark Paris Agreement in 2015 , to try to limit global warming . <p> But , while the hot year certainly is n't good news , this breach of 1.5C does n't mean we 've broken the Paris Agreement . <p> Let 's break down why that is , what it means for our climate and weather , and where 1.5C marker came from in the first place . <h> What is the Paris Agreement ? <p> The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change . <p> It was the first time that almost all countries agreed to work together to limit global warming and adapt to climate change , with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ demand the government take action on climate change . ( Photo by Mark Metcalfe/Getty Images ) <p> As a part of the agreement , countries agreed to substantially reduce global greenhouse gas emissions to keep the long-term global average surface temperature to " well below 2C " above pre-industrial levels . <p> They also agreed to " pursue efforts " to limit warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial times , using the years between 1850-1900 as the baseline . <h> What does 1.5 degrees of warming mean ? <p> An increase of 1.5C or 2C may seem small on the surface . After all , you do n't really notice the difference between a 27C and 29C day . <p> But Professor David Karoly , a climate scientist at the University of Melbourne and the Climate Council , said an increase of 1.5C on a global scale meant many more extremely hot days on the ground . <p> " 1.5C of global warming also means more that 2C of warming over land areas , which is where people live , " he said . <p> Professor David Karoly from the University @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : David Karoly ) <p> The 1.5C target was chosen because the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) indicates that crossing that threshold risks unleashing far more severe climate change impacts , including more frequent and severe droughts , heatwaves , rainfall , and coastal flooding from storm surges . <p> Professor Karoly said no level of global warming was absolutely safe , however . <p> " We 've seen that with the impacts of climate change over the last 10 and 20 years already . @@119951622 <p> The world has watched in horror as fires continue to raze parts of Los Angeles , California . For those of us living in Australia , one of the world 's most fire-prone continents , the LA experience feels all too familiar . <p> A " perfect storm " of several factors resulted in the catastrophic fires now burning in Southern California : long-term climate change combined with extreme weather conditions , all playing out in one of the most densely populated parts of the United States . <p> The tragedy offers valuable lessons for other global cities in a similar climate zone to Los Angeles -- including the Australian centres of Adelaide and Perth . The fires are also instructive for centres such as Sydney and Melbourne , where the climate is warming and drying . <p> That 's why , in Australia , it 's important to understand how climate drivers played out before and during the LA wildfire emergency . Some are naturally occurring and others are the result of global warming . So let 's look at them in more detail . <h> How climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Earth 's water cycle is changing . Over the past 50 years , this has led to an expansion of Earth 's tropical and subtropical zones . Tropical areas are moist and lush , but dry at the northern and southern edges . <p> These dry edges are pushing towards the poles . Regions that used to enjoy a gentler Mediterranean climate , as shown in the map below , are turning into dry subtropical zones . <p> As the shift continues , winter rainfall in these regions is largely declining . In the case of California , this decline has mostly occurred in southern areas of the state which are closer to the dry subtropical edge . <p> The expansion of the tropics means rainfall in California has also become more erratic . Since the 1980s it has endured years of abnormally high rain and snow , followed by years of very low rain and snow . This variability has been dubbed " climate whiplash " . <p> The exceptionally wet years fuelled widespread vegetation growth . This growth shrivelled in the dry years , providing ample fuel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the proportion of rain versus snow has increased in the Sierra Nevada and Southern Cascades regions of the state . <p> The climate of Melbourne and Sydney has historically been classed as " warm temperate " rather than Mediterranean , with some rain in all months of the year . But both have experienced warming and moderate drying since the 1980s . <p> If current climate trends continue , by 2100 the edge of the new dry subtropical zone would extend across the continent in a rough band from Sydney to Perth . <p> La Ni ? a usually brings drought to Southern California . On this occasion , that part of the state was already very dry . This is consistent with the " climate whiplash " effect described above . <p> As others have noted , in early January the soil moisture in much of Southern California was in the bottom 2% of historical records . This dryness helped propel the fires . <p> During an El Ni ? o , Australia typically becomes hotter and drier , and the bushfire risk increases . We saw this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which followed the 2018 -- 19 El Ni ? o . <h> The notorious Santa Ana winds <p> The Santa Ana winds are a natural phenomenon that typically occur during the southern California autumn and into January . They rush from the top of the San Gabriel Mountains , in northern Los Angeles County , and head towards the coast , warming and drying the landscape . <p> The canyons and steep cliffs in the Los Angeles region also drive these gusty winds across exposed areas of land -- many densely populated . <p> Australia does not have a direct equivalent to the Santa Ana winds . But the continent does experience hot , dry winds much larger in scale . They originate from the arid centre and blow towards the coast , often driving bushfires . <h> What all this means for Australia <p> The horrific fires in California may be rare . But disasters of this scale are likely in future as climate change worsens . Most Mediterranean climate regions will experience a 5 -- 10% decline in precipitation this century . That increases the bushfire risk .

@@119993188 <h> The decades-long drying trend that increased fire risk in the US Southwest <h> Save articles for later <p> The American Southwest is the driest it has been since the year 800 after a decade-long " megadrought " , creating tinderbox conditions that underlie the catastrophic fires in Los Angeles . <p> The heavy rain events of the past two winters in California were not enough to disrupt the long-term drying trend , and there has been barely a drop this winter . <p> Andrew J. Kruczkiewicz , a climate scientist at Columbia University , said the data showed the desert areas west of the Rocky Mountains and into Southern California had dried out over the past half-century . <p> The drier conditions increased the risk of bushfires , he said , though further analysis would be needed to definitively say the Los Angeles fires were caused by climate change . <p> " When we 're talking about wildfire risk -- and in Australia , the ingredients are very similar -- you need low relative humidity , you need drier than average conditions or dry conditions , and you need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the primary meteorological factors that lead to wildfire risk ... not necessarily ignition of wildfires , but the spread . So the ingredients are there . " <p> Southern California , Nevada , Arizona , Utah , New Mexico , and parts of Colorado and Texas are in drought , figures from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration ( NOAA ) show . Western Texas is in " exceptional drought " , the highest level . <p> The last time Los Angeles had rainfall of more than 2.54 millimetres was May last year , as this masthead reported last week . Only months before , in February , nearly 30 centimetres of rain hit the University of California , Los Angeles , in just two days . Scientists have described this oscillation between wet and dry as " hydroclimate whiplash " . <p> Advertisement <p> The drought is not a new phenomenon . An article in Nature Climate Change , led by researchers at the University of California , Los Angeles , in February 2022 , labelled the period since 2000 a " megadrought " because it was so prolonged @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ region west of the Rocky Mountains from southern Montana to northern Mexico from 800 to 1600 , followed by a 400-year hiatus . <p> Human-caused climate change is responsible for about 42 per cent of the soil moisture deficit since 2000 , the paper found , because warmer temperatures are increasing evaporation , which dries out soil and vegetation . From 2000 to 2021 , temperatures in the region were 0.91 degrees higher than the average from 1950 to 1999 . <p> The Palmer Drought Severity Index , based on NOAA figures published by the US Environment Protection Agency , suggests a long-term drying trend for six states in the Southwest over the 20th and 21st centuries . The index took average annual rainfall for Arizona , California , Colorado , Nevada , New Mexico and Utah . <p> The figures show several long dry spells followed by periods that are wetter than average since 1895 when the records began . But the period from the beginning of 1999 to the end of 2023 was the driest of the dry spells in the records -- 20 times drier on average @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1949-1973 . <p> Kruczkiewicz said there were seasonal and regional variations within the drying trend . In California , the biggest drop in rainfall in California was in the September to November period , while the trend was weaker in December to February . <p> There were also other natural forces at play , Kruczkiewicz said , such as the El Nino-La Nina southern oscillation . La Nina causes wetter , rainier conditions in Australia but warmer , drier conditions on the US West Coast , and vice versa for El Nino.

@@119994620 <p> This work was funded by the Victorian Government Department of Energy , Environment and Climate Action ( DEECA ) in collaboration with the U.S. Forest Service , Pacific Northwest Research Station , Portland , Oregon USA . <p> The recent LA fires are emblematic of fire behaviour changing in unexpected ways . These fires , occurring during winter and outside the traditional fire season also follow an extremely hot summer and prolonged drought in California . <p> While the winds driving the LA fires are not uncommon , the lack of precipitation preceding them was extreme and similar drought events are likely to become more frequent as climate change intensifies . As these conditions become more frequent , we can expect that wildfire regimes are going to change . <p> Protecting people and the environment is not as simple as fighting fires when they happen . Picture : Getty Images <p> Wildfire regimes -- the patterns of fire activity over time -- are now shaped by two major forces : climate change and human actions ( both through intentional fire management programs and through continued habitat destruction or alterations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up causing an increased risk to people , property , and the environment . <p> Protecting people and the environment is not as simple as fighting fires when they happen . It requires strategic planning , proactive and innovative management , and critically , understanding the trade-offs between values . <h> More than just fighting flames <p> Fire management is extremely diverse , but the two main approaches are fuel management and suppression ( also known as firefighting ) <p> Fuel managementinvolves altering the amount and structure of flammable material in a landscape , often through prescribed burns or mechanical treatments . These strategies aim to lower fire intensity and rate of spread by simplifying fuels <p> Suppression focuses on controlling and containing fires once they start , as well as protecting assets like buildings , roads and powerlines by deploying people , fire trucks and aircraft to slow or stop the fires and in turn reduce damage . <p> But neither approach alone is a silver bullet . <p> Fuel management requires careful planning and is often constrained by weather conditions , public perception and considerations of key trade-offs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of fire management <p> Our research explored this problem for regions in Victoria by combining climate data , fire simulations and cost data to develop a framework for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of various fire management strategies now and into the future . <p> We developed a model designed to capture uncertainty and evaluate the outcomes of hypothetical fire management strategies under varying climate scenarios . <p> This approach enabled us to analyse data from over 1,200 fire regime simulations , covering 16 modelled management strategies across six regions and six climate models . <p> This meant we could characterise a range of potential future outcomes and evaluate them against one another for current and future conditions . <p> As the climate continues to warm , even the best strategies face mounting challenges . Picture : Getty Images <p> The model evaluates how management strategies affected risk to key assets , including people and property , infrastructure , agricultural production and environmental services . <p> From this data , we determined the cost-effectiveness of each strategy by weighing the expense of implementing fire management programs against the reduction in economic impacts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ management strategies were considered equally effective . <p> The most cost-effective approaches generally combined prescribed burning and suppression . These strategies varied significantly between regions , but generally reduced wildfire impacts more efficiently than doing nothing or the most intensive interventions ( i.e. throwing everything we have at it ) . <p> Doing nothing is not a cost-effective option . <p> Under current and worsening climate conditions , the cost of inaction was consistently higher than any management strategy . <p> These costs are all impacts on societal values and the environment . Wildfires which are left unmanaged under changing climate led to severe damage and skyrocketing costs , resulting in losses to communities and ecosystems . <p> This was considerably worse under future climate projections . <p> The cost of inaction is consistently higher than any management strategy . Picture : Getty Images <p> Conversely , strategies that involve high levels of burning or excessive fuel management do not deliver a cost-effective program either . This is because of the elevated costs to environmental values and human health , primarily through the negative impacts of smoke . <p> It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will lead to greater costs -- financial , social and environmental . <p> We need to rethink how we manage fire in a changing climate . <p> No single strategy can eliminate wildfire risks , but combining science , strategic planning and adaptive management offers the best path forward . <p> By prioritising cost-effective actions now , that have longevity under future conditions , we can reduce impacts , protect vital assets and ensure a safer future for communities on the frontlines of fire and climate change . <h> Follow Pursuit <p> Social media <h> Acknowledgement of country <p> We acknowledge Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as the Traditional Owners of the unceded lands on which we work , learn and live .
