@@119994633 <p> A 2024 study by researchers based at the University of Bristol sports a highly pertinent title for Australian policymakers : Criminalisation and Repression of Climate and Environmental Protest . <p> It examines the pressing patterns of criminalisation and repression of climate and environmental protest around the world and the various laws and powers that have been introduced and used to that end . The report is informed by Armed Conflict Location &amp; Event Data ( ACLED ) and the non-government entity Global Witness . <p> Of the 14 countries that receive an in-depth examination , Australia receives particular attention . The authors note Australia as " an exception among all 14 countries included in this study in having ... both a high percentage of both climate ( 12.9% ) and other environmental protests ( 3.8% ) . " <p> This is unsurprising given the commanding role extractive industries continue to exercise in the country . Despite the renewables agenda being promoted by the Albanese government , mining extensions continue to be approved . <p> On December 19 , for instance , Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek approved three such projects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ same day , she also boasted that the Labor government was in the process of " turning Australia into a renewable superpower . " <p> The fossil fuel lobby , with the aid of state premiers , keeps a watchful eye on environmental changes that pose a risk to earnings and profits . ( The scuppering of the proposed federal Environmental Protection Agency by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the face of concerns from Western Australia was a striking example of this . ) <p> In the face of perceived tardiness on the climate change front , the environmental defender has emerged as a challenge to lawmakers and bureaucrats . They include , according to Michel Forst , UN Special Rapporteur on Environmental Defenders under the Aarhus Convention , " Any member of the public seeking to protect the right to live in an environment adequate to their health and wellbeing " . <p> Given the urgency posed by the threat of climate change , and the " inadequate response from governments " , the peaceful protest , according to Forst , has found expression in various ways , including @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " . These include the now familiar practices of occupying construction sites , the use of slow marches , and the deployment of roadblocks to cause traffic jams . <p> Adopting a punitive policy to such protests serves , according to the Bristol report , a fundamental purpose : shifting the focus away from inadequate responses to the agents of climate change in favour of penalising those who oppose inaction in the face of it . Such policies , according to the authors , are authoritarian in nature and fundamentally inconsistent " with the ideals of vibrant civil societies in liberal democracies . " <p> The study notes responses to such environmental defenders of varying severity . In the global south , governments , sometimes aided by corporate actors , have resorted to instances of extreme violence , including killing activists . The non-government organisation Global Witness reports that 2,106 killings took place between 2012 and 2023 , primarily in such countries as Colombia , Brazil , Peru , Mexico , Honduras and the Philippines . <p> Australian environment protestors , unlike their counterparts in the global south , have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ form of censorship . Instead , their movements and expression are being increasingly limited by the passage of new laws across the various states , the use of pre-existing laws intended to punish rather different offences , otherwise described as " secondary criminalisation " and increasingly high rates of arrest . Since 2019 , the states of Queensland , NSW , Tasmania , Victoria and South Australia have all passed legislation as refurbishments to existing laws to curb protest . <p> In its 2021 report , Australia 's Environmental Defenders Office ( EDO ) , in collaboration with the Human Rights Law Centre and Greenpeace , affirms similar trends , including the increasing use of strategic lawsuits against public participation ( SLAPP ) by governments and extractive firms . Environmental groups have also been the target of excessive penalties and the novel use of bail conditions to limit participation in protests . <p> While environmental defenders and activists are often demonised as privileged and deluded ( former prime minister Scott Morrison used the derisory term " un-Australian green criminals " ) , their rights to assemble and gather to protest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Despite lacking a fundamental human rights charter , Australia remains a signatory to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ( ICCPR ) , which recognises the right to freedom of association . A number of international instruments enunciate the same principle , accompanied by weak common law traditions on the subject . Even Australia 's High Court has recognised , if only in very limited form , an implied constitutional right to communication on political subjects . Being less a personal right than a restraint on legislative power , litigants have had some success in using it to target anti-protest laws , most notably in the 2017 case of Brown v Tasmania . The legislative and policy trend is , however , clear : the ledger remains heavily stacked against environmental activists who wish to take to public spaces to opine and demonstrate .

@@120037560 <p> The Moon is one of 25 sites to be concerned about this year , according to a leading cultural heritage watchdog organization . <p> That organization is the World Monuments Fund , which today announced the 25 sites on its annual World Monuments Watch . The sites were selected from over 200 nominations that underwent two review cycles before selection by an independent panel of experts . The Moon stands apart from the rest as a cultural heritage site that is not on Earth . <p> " For the first time , the Moon is included on the Watch to reflect the urgent need to recognize and preserve the artifacts that testify to humanity 's first steps beyond Earth -- a defining moment in our shared history , " said B ? n ? dicte de Montlaur , the president and CEO of the fund , in an organization release . <p> " Items such as the camera that captured the televised moon landing ; a memorial disk left by astronauts Armstrong and Aldrin ; and hundreds of other objects are emblematic of this legacy , " de Montlaur @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accelerating lunar activities , undertaken without adequate preservation protocols . " <p> There are over 90 historic sites on the Moon where spacecraft have made contact with the lunar surface , the release noted . One of the most famous artifacts are astronauts ' first footprints beyond Earth , made by the Apollo 11 astronauts in 1969 . <p> " As we embark on a new era of space exploration , we must ensure that the traces of these extraordinary milestones in humanity 's history -- the first moon landings -- are preserved , " the release stated . " The inclusion of the Moon on the 2025 Watch advocates for international agreements and protections for lunar heritage sites and invites a broader public conversation on what this new Space Age might mean for the Moon 's cultural and natural landscape . " <p> The Moon 's inclusion on the list is a prudent one , as humankind intends to return to the Moon and stay there for the long term . NASA 's Artemis mission plans to put a crewed mission on the lunar surface by mid-2027 -- though @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that 's just the tip of the iceberg , as a host of private missions , many funded through NASA 's Commercial Lunar Payload Services ( CLPS ) initiative , are planned in the coming months and years . Just this morning , for example , SpaceX launched a pair of landers to the Moon , namely Firefly Aerospace 's Blue Ghost lander and ispace 's Resilience lander . <p> SpaceX 's Starship is also in the mix -- NASA 's chosen lander for Artemis missions , yet ultimately a privately owned vessel that could one day ferry tourists to the Moon and its many historic sites . <p> Plans are also in the works to mine the Moon for its various resources , including water ice , helium-3 , and rare earth elements ( REEs ) . Some private ventures are also hoping to use the Moon as a kind of graveyard , in which the remains of loved ones are plopped onto the dusty surface . Needless to say , the Moon will never be the same again , prompting the World Monuments Fund to voice its concerns @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or flowing water on its surface , so natural degradation of lunar artifacts has not been a problem . In fact , the lunar surface is immaculately preserved . But " exploitative visitation , souveniring , and looting by future missions and private lunar exploration could eventually compromise this truly unique cultural heritage , removing artifacts and forever erasing iconic prints and tracks from the Moon 's surface , " the fund warns on its landing page for the Moon . <p> Other sites on the World Monument Fund 's list this year include those damaged by conflict and natural disaster , such as the historic city of Antakya ( ancient Antioch ) in Turkey , which was devastated by earthquakes in 2023 , and Gaza 's historic urban fabric , which is on the receiving end of ongoing Israeli airstrikes . <p> Sites on the list that are under threat from climate change are Africa 's Swahili Coast and Maine 's historic lighthouses . Other sites include the monasteries in Albania 's Drino Valley -- under pressure from over-tourism -- France 's Chapel of the Sorbonne in Paris , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in India 's Musi River , which suffers from pervasive pollution issues . <p> Cultural heritage needs protection from a range of threats , both natural and anthropogenic . In 2023 , Greenpeace experts found that 4th-century Buddhist murals in China were being damaged by heavy rain and humidity . Last year , a group of researchers from the University of Virginia found evidence that the Russian military is damaging Ukrainian archaeological sites during its occupation of the country . <p> The World Monuments Fund 's full list of 25 sites for 2025 can be found on the organization 's website , but it is ( obviously ) not comprehensive . Though we 've said goodbye to 2024 , plenty of the sites featured in last year 's list remain under threat , many from the same causes that are endangering this year 's sites .

@@120038237 <h> It 's the S-Curve , stupid : New model predicts half of world 's energy will come from solar by 2035 <p> In the hazy first weeks of 2025 -- with Los Angeles burning , Trump headed back to the White House , and Australia approaching an election that could be disastrous for climate and renewables -- solar PV remains an unbroken ray of hope . <p> This remarkable technology , which owes a good deal of its modern success to Australian researchers and universities , dominates the new energy landscape all around the globe , growing at a rate that continues to defy expectations , all the while becoming cheaper , more efficient and faster to deploy . <p> According to estimates from the Global Solar Council and SolarPower Europe , the world reached the stunning cumulative total of 2 terawatts ( TW ) of installed solar capacity in November last year -- a milestone that came just two years after the first terawatt mark , which took 68 years to notch up . <p> In Australia , rooftop solar alone regularly supplies the majority of daytime power @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is gearing up to do the same . <p> In New South Wales , utility-scale solar generated more than 40 per cent of the state 's power for the first time in the first week of January -- a remarkable milestone for one of Australia 's biggest remaining coal power holdouts . <p> But can solar keep up the pace ? Or rather , can solar growth ramp up to the levels needed to triple renewables and meet increasingly urgent climate targets ? <p> According to a newly launched climate modeling tool , the answer to these questions is a resounding ' yes ' -- or , more accurately , ' you ai n't seen nothin ' yet . ' <p> The S-Curve model , developed by Australian solar industry pioneer Andrew Birch , predicts that by 2035 , half of the world 's energy needs will be supplied by solar in a classic S-curve technology shift . <p> Image source : Andrew Birch <p> The S-Curve projects forward solar 's historical trends , predicting that it will continue to fall in cost by 10% a year and grow at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nuclear power this year and eclipse oil by 2031 . <p> " On current growth trends , solar is on track to displace 50 per cent of traditional energy supply within a decade , " says Birch , a UNSW PV engineering graduate and founding member of some of the leading global solar companies over the last 20 years , including OpenSolar . <p> " This should scare you if you 're still financing coal , oil or gas , " he adds . <p> Birch 's theory is that " three huge mistakes " -- including a flawed equation at the heart of solar projections -- have resulted in decades of inaccurate energy market forecasting on solar . <p> The first mistake , he says in a video on his newly launched website here , is the belief that solar cost reductions are " suddenly going to stop from nowhere . " The second mistaken assumption is that the market 's consistent growth of well over 25 per cent a year will also suddenly end . <p> " I 've seen the analysts call the end to this high @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wrong again and again and again , " Birch says . <p> The final mistake Birch describes as more of an accounting problem . " We 're told by traditional energy brains that we need a certain amount of energy to run our economy , but over half of that fossil fuel energy is wasted when we burn it in our homes , cars and power plants , " he says . <p> The S-Curve seeks to correct this by using delivered energy as the metric underpinning projections , rather than primary energy . In this way , the projections show a solar electric economy will require 60% less energy than previously assumed . <p> " Solar 's learning curve has never ended , " says Birch . " In fact , its growth rate has increased . When you combine this growth trend with the lower energy needed with electrification you get a solar-dominated system within just 10 years . " <p> " Birchy , " as he calls himself , has a long and distinguished solar pedigree , having abandoned his first career choice , investment banking , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the University of New South Wales . <p> He then joined BP Solar , where he developed world-first PV financing solutions and designed the " feed-in tariff " model that kick-started the Australian solar market . <p> A decade or so later , Birch and Pryor started OpenSolar , the world 's first free solar software retailing and installation platform that has amassed more than 25,000 users in more than 150 countries . <p> Currently , Birch is based in the UK where he has been collaborating with Professor Andrew Crossland at the Durham University Energy Institute on the best ways to support the growth of solar around the world , and to use solar electrification to benefit consumers . The pair has co-authored a white paper for Ed Miliband , the UK 's Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero . <p> According to Birch , to solve the climate crisis , installed solar capacity needs to grow at a rate of 25% per annum . @@120038268 <h> Nothing new under the sun : A long history of missed chances to build sustainable homes <p> Australians are no strangers to housing crises . Some will even remember the crisis that followed the second world war . As well as producing the popular mid-century modern style of architecture , these post-war decades were a time of struggle . <p> As the population grew quickly after the war , Australia faced an estimated shortage of 300,000 dwellings . Government intervention was needed . A 1944 report by the Commonwealth Housing Commission stated that " a dwelling of good standard and equipment is not only the need but the right of every citizen " . <p> A key recommendation was that the Australian government should encourage the building of more climate-responsive and healthy homes . <h> Building small and for a sunny climate <p> The postwar period was a time of shortages and rationing . As well as meat , sugar , clothing and fuel , building materials were in short supply . <p> Government restrictions limited house sizes in general to around 110 square metres . That 's less @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Building activity and the prices of materials were also regulated . <p> While people waited for building permits , many had to arrange temporary housing . Some lived in sleepouts or rented spare rooms from strangers . Others camped in tents or lived in caravans or temporary buildings erected on land bought before the war . <p> Looking at the published advice on housing design in the 1940s and 1950s , it 's clear passive solar design , small home sizes and climate-responsive architecture were topics of interest . A passive solar design works with the local climate to maintain a comfortable temperature in the home . <p> A typical builder 's house plan of the post-war period , ' This Week 's Plan ' from The Builder , March 20 1953 . Architecture Museum , University of South Australia <p> This preference was not driven by concerns about climate change or carbon footprints . Rather , the Commonwealth Housing Commission called for solar planning " for health and comfort " . <p> The commission 's executive officer , architect Walter Bunning , demonstrated how to go about this in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recommendations into a format appealing to home builders . <p> This was a time before most home owners could afford air conditioning . It was advised that homes be sited to capture prevailing breezes , have insulated walls and roofs , use window shading and overhanging eaves , and plantings of shade trees and deciduous creepers . External spaces , such as patios , and north-facing living spaces oriented to the sun , were also promoted . <p> Among the designs were plans for the " Sun Trap House " . This design applied passive solar design principles to a modest freestanding home . <h> ' New approach ' did n't eventuate <p> Eventually , the housing crisis eased . However , this was not a result of Bunning 's hoped for " new approach to house planning " . Most of the new housing was traditionally designed and built suburban homes . <p> Architect 's plan from Small Homes Service of South Australia brochure.Cheesman collection S209 , Architecture Museum , University of South Australia <h> Passive solar solutions are timeless <p> The energy-hungry mechanical heating and cooling of today @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as insulation , eaves , window awnings , curtains and draught stoppers . These were common solutions in the post-war period . <p> The principles of passive solar design have n't changed since then . The ideas advocated both in 1945 and today in design advice such as the Australian government 's Your Home guide to environmentally sustainable homes remain the same . <p> A house built from Plan AC 301 by the Small Homes Service of South Australia , 1959 . Tideman collection S307 , Architecture Museum , University of South Australia <p> While our world today faces many crises affecting health , climate resilience , housing affordability and inequality , we have a chance to shape the solutions .

" <p> Prior to the amendment , no action had been taken against landholders during fire emergencies , however the state government has said it wanted to fix the issue to ensure peace of mind . <p> " We recognise landholders need to access water quickly when preparing for or fighting a fire and it 's not practical to fill out paperwork for this basic safety measure , " a NSW Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water spokesperson said . <p> " These changes are a result of extensive feedback from farmers and other stakeholders about the challenges they face when protecting life and property . " <p> People wanting to prepare for the threat of bush fires will be able to take water and store it elsewhere for future emergencies as well , such as in tanks and dams , with the maximum volume for each property limited to 100,000 litres per year . <h> Hopeful for more change <p> Mr Bootle hopes this amendment is a step towards the review of stock and domestic entitlement under the water act . <p> He believes the act is currently too narrow , and with this amendment now in place , he would like to see some other definitions changed . <p> " It needs to not just be water for firefighting , but water for crop spraying - that currently is potentially a breach of the regulations , " Mr Bootle said . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first of a series of sensible steps that this government will do for farmers . " <p> While landholders have no obligation to log the volume of water they take under the exemption , the state government encourages the record taking for their own knowledge . <p> " We will carry out targeted periodic surveys of landholders to identify the extent and scale of water used for firefighting and fire preparedness , " a DCCEEW spokesperson said . <p> " This will enable us to better understand how the exemptions are being used and inform a three to five-year review ... which will look into whether the exemptions should be maintained , modified or transitioned to a new form of basic landholder water right . @@120081001 <h> 73,700 lightning strikes : How the storm that stunned Sydney exploded <h> Save articles for later <p> A stewing Sydney summer evening broke in spectacular fashion on Wednesday with a storm emblematic of the hotter , wetter , more humid summer predicted for much of Australia by the Bureau of Meteorology . <p> At 8.25pm , the dew point temperature -- a direct measure of water in the air -- surpassed 22 degrees , well past the threshold that feels horribly muggy . <p> A line of storms track east over Homebush.Credit : Wolter Peeters <p> But then the humidity snapped with a rainstorm that belted the city with 24 millimetres of rain in 19 minutes . <p> Lightning flashes lit up the deluge -- 73,700 strikes flared within 100 kilometres of the CBD , according to Weatherzone , and 8777 struck the ground . <p> Two million lightning strikes hit Australia as a continent-spanning line of storms roared over battered towns from Tasmania to Queensland . <p> " It 's one of the most lightning-intense storms that I 've ever seen , " said Sydney climate scientist Dr @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change in this generation of severe storms . <p> Lightning over NSW during the storms that thrashed the east coast on Wednesday night.Credit : Weatherzone.com.au <p> The basic ingredients for thunderstorms are moisture and rapidly rising air . <p> " Air near the surface is warm , and up higher in the atmosphere , it 's cooler . If a little bit of that warm air gets into the cold air , then it rises like a hot air balloon , and it causes updraughts to form , " said Raupach , from the University of NSW . <p> Advertisement <p> Storm clouds condense if there 's enough moisture in the air for the updraught to draw on . Add twists and turns in wind speed and direction -- called wind shear -- and a chaotic supercell storm can form . <p> The more violently wind shear destabilises a storm system , the more lightning is unleashed , as differences between positively and negatively charged regions of a cloud grow more dramatic . <p> 73,700 lightning strikes were recorded within 100km of Sydney between midday and midnight on Wednesday.Credit : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ field day , with Sydneysiders reporting flying trampolines , branches smashing cars and a tornado-like squall whipping through Moorebank . <p> " The air pressure in Sydney got down to 992 , which is incredibly low , " said the owner of the page , longtime weather observer and storm-chaser Paul . " Those are the sort of pressures you 'd find associated with a developing tropical cyclone , for example . And that was over land . <p> " Troughs are the Earth 's ability to manage its heat budget . It 's trying to drag down hot air from the tropics to the poles , and in return , it shunts up cold air from the poles , from Antarctica . <p> Lightning seen from Anzac Memorial Bridge in Newcastle.Credit : Getty Images <p> " What we saw yesterday was a dynamic , dramatic attempt by the atmosphere to try and balance that budget . " <p> The storm was so severe because a phenomenal amount of warm air rocketed high into a cold region of the atmosphere , generating storm clouds which unleashed the atmospheric light show @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the lightning is what you normally get in the tropics . What I observed yesterday was that a lot of the cloud heights were above 16 kilometres -- that 's significant , " Paul said . " In Sydney , it was definitely unique and rare . " <p> A section of a roof from townhouses in Carlingford lays on a garden area after Wednesday night 's storm.Credit : Kate Geraghty <p> The effect of climate change on storms is a matter of ongoing scientific investigation . But the average intensity of rain unleashed by thunderstorms in Australia has increased by about 27 per cent in the past four decades , according to a paper by Melbourne climatologist Associate Professor Andrew Dowdy . <p> The atmosphere 's spongelike ability to soak up moisture is increasing by 7 per cent for every degree of warming , meaning that when it rains , it 's far more likely to pour . <p> " When there 's more water there , there 's more energy that can be released as that water condenses , and you can get a more vigorous storm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ said . <p> " A hailstone that spends a long time growing in the storm , because it can be held up by an updraught for a really long time , is going to end up a lot bigger . " <p> Raupach 's previous research revealed the number of hail-prone days in Sydney has spiked by 40 per cent over the last two decades . <p> Days prone to hail have increased by 40 per cent in Sydney.Credit : Edwina Pickles <p> However , warmer temperatures mean hail also melts faster . So we may see less frequent hailstorms all up , but when they do strike , it 's likely to be the more damaging stones large enough to make it to the ground . <p> The bureau predicted a hot , wet , humid summer in October . Last year was the hottest on record , weather agencies confirmed last week , and surpassed 1.5 degrees of warming .

Over the last decade , he 's reviewed phones for TechRadar as well as covered tech , gaming , and culture for Engadget , Popular Mechanics , NBC Asian America , Increment , Fast Company and others . As a true Californian , he lives for coffee , beaches and burritos . <p> The view from what 's left of Will Rogers State Park , burned in the Palisades Fire in Los Angeles . <p> Apu Gomes/Getty Images <p> Every January , CES is meant to be a showcase of the tech trends that will shape the coming year . While the annual tech trade show is known for its pie-in-the-sky futuristic concepts -- from rollable screens to flying vehicles -- this year 's show felt particularly out of touch . Whereas CES 2024 's techno-futuristic forecasting was balanced by progressive promises for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2025 was remarkably quiet on efforts to preserve the planet . <p> While the year 's biggest tech show promoted $7,000 coffee makers , humanoid robots and eye-popping TVs , wildfires ripped through the northern and western edges of one of the world 's most populous cities -- and the one I live in . As we learned about the future of technology against the backdrop of flashy casino lights and elaborate cocktail parties , over 10,000 homes burned to ash in Los Angeles , as people in my city lost everything from their present and their past . <p> Catastrophic weather events aside , the tech industry is n't exactly known for being sustainable . The smartphones I write excitedly about are made of rare earth elements mined in deplorable conditions by modern-day slaves , as NPR has reported . Well over a decade after the first news broke of suicides occurring in the Foxconn facilities in China where iPhones are made , reports continue to emerge on the brutal conditions of assembly lines for today 's devices . A 2023 report from Rest of World details manufacturing realities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and a story from Hankyoreh last year sheds light on women workers who went on strike after mangling their fingers on the Samsung phone production lines in the Giheung district of Yongin , South Korea . <p> But I 'm newly despondent that even the modicum of sustainability on show at last year 's CES 2024 was significantly downplayed . Sustainability has never been the sexiest topic , with companies frequently tucking their eco-commitments into the closing moments of their presentations . @@120082458 <p> The fires in Los Angeles are estimated to be the most expensive disaster in US history at US$250 -- 275 billion , or 24 to 26 percent of Australia 's annual GDP . That loss has accrued in just over a week and is rising . <p> This was not a natural disaster . That would imply a lack of human responsibility . Rather , this is what happens when a human-warmed climate catches us off-guard -- even in a city that knows fire . <p> Australia has done significant work since the 2019 -- 20 Black Summer fires , and the floods that followed , to appreciate climate risks and prepare for them . However , much of that work , including the National Climate Risk Assessment and the National Adaptation Plan , is yet to be released . As the federal election nears , all parties should remind themselves to not treat climate as a political football -- a priority only when disasters strike or when it 's convenient . <p> These events will continue to surprise if we fail to understand and address the locked-in disaster @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cause greater loss if we continue warming the atmosphere . <p> While climate change is n't the only factor in play in LA , it 's a big part of why officials were taken by surprise . Compound climate-amplified disasters build quietly but strike swiftly . In this case climate appears to have primed the intensity of the fires . <p> California is no stranger to whiplashing climate conditions . It experienced a three-year drought from 2020 to 2022 , followed by two years of significant rainfall -- recording LA 's seventh-wettest year in 2022 -- 23 . That rainfall drove vegetation growth , then a sustained drought and higher than average temperatures at the start of the current winter dried much of that new vegetation . <p> The Santa Ana winds that fanned the flames with hot , dry air are typical for the area in winter but were particularly strong with gusts at nearly 160km/h last week -- at times grounding firefighting aircraft when they were needed most , pushing fires faster down hillsides where they 'd normally slow , and spewing embers far beyond firelines . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ temperatures and a meandering North American jet stream , which has been increasingly disrupted by climate change in recent years and may have also contributed to the atmospheric rivers dumping rain over LA in the years before the fires . <p> Clear answers on the origins of the fires will come once investigations conclude . Speculating now does n't help . Misinformation abounds online , as it increasingly does after disasters , with harmful effects on responders , confusing the response and muddying the analysis needed for future preparation . For example , conspiracy theories hold that the US government used weather control to intensify Hurricane Helene -- which struck the southeast United States in September last year -- to cause widespread damage . That led to Federal Emergency Management Agency responders facing armed threats . <p> The Eaton fire , the second-largest in LA , may have been sparked by damaged electrical infrastructure from powerful Santa Ana winds , as has happened in the past . If that 's the case , it adds more pressure to California 's ongoing efforts to prepare its infrastructure for intensifying natural disasters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but risks remain -- in part because there are no cheap solutions . By California 's own estimates , burying all distribution and transmission lines in the state could cost US$763 billion -- roughly 70 percent of Australia 's 2024 GDP -- and would take years . Nonetheless , the economics of such climate adaptation has become clearer since just a single week of fire has reached a third of that cost . <p> Urban development has also played a role . Malibu and the surrounding area are traditional fire country -- the chaparral vegetation evolved to undergo periods of fire . But there are now eight million people living in fire-prone areas in southern California . Fire-resilient building designs as well as fuel reduction and landscaping around houses might have slowed the growth of the fires in urban environments , protecting more homes . There is no easy way to get around the consequences of building and living in high risk areas ; all we can do is try to avoid it in future . <p> Even though many affected communities are aware of climate and fire risk , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with fire resilience in mind will be necessary , especially as fire insurance will become unaffordable for many . <p> While much focus has been on insufficient water supplies to fight the fires , most reservoirs were full -- contradicting misinformation that California 's environmental planning restricted access to upstream sources . <p> A more plausible explanation for California 's underpreparedness is that urban water infrastructure simply is n't designed for wildfire . <p> The Pacific Palisades neighbourhood , where many celebrities lost their homes , is at the end of the local water line , so receives less water pressure . As hydrants were tapped for water , the pressure dropped , draining emergency tanks in the neighbourhood . <p> An investigation will assess the reasons for , and effect of , the ongoing closure of the Santa Ynez reservoir in the Palisades area -- hopefully including why it was n't rapidly brought back online late in 2024 as climate conditions worsened . <p> That brings us to the funding , staffing and preparation of LA 's fire authorities . Attention focused on the mayor 's budget reductions , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year . While that may have had an effect , clearly the scale of the need was far beyond a few percentage points . <p> Inadequate staffing was a pressure early on , even with 9000 firefighters in LA County alone . <p> That is n't a cheap solve , either . If LA needs greater capacity on hand at any time , its budget would have to grow significantly . That demand would have to compete with resources needed to prepare for and reduce the risk of future fires , including potential private firefighting capacities . Again , early investment in preparedness will reduce the complications in and need for future reactive responses . But building out future response capacity will take time . <p> The bottom line is that LA 's various failures in preparation means it was caught off-guard , but this disaster would n't have been so extreme without climate disruption priming such an intense and unexpected set of fires . <p> The same dynamic has occurred in Australia , and it will continue if we do n't take climate risks seriously . These events are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ painful , but also entirely predictable . <p> Author <p> Mike Copage is head of the Climate and Security Policy Centre at ASPI.

Hu Xijin , former editor of the most nationalistic Chinese newspaper @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for China to expand its global outreach . The massive migration from TikTok to Red has also been reported favourably in China 's state media . <p> Let 's look at the opportunities for Red and the Chinese state , apart from the obvious economic ones : Red would benefit greatly from a significant increase in foreign traffic , which would only grow if the proposed TikTok ban goes ahead . <p> The influx of TikTok refugees brings with it two crucial attractions . First , the arrival of ordinary American people brings a previously unavailable target audience over which China can seek to exert its soft power . China 's " Going Global " strategy of exporting state media content to the Western world , which was initiated in the 1990s , has mostly failed to achieve its soft power goals . <p> This has left the Chinese government scratching its head trying to figure out how to access ordinary members of the public in the West . A US decision to ban TikTok could thus be a blessing in disguise , creating an unprecedented channel for communication and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ previously . <p> Many Western TikTok users have been posting about their experiences of travelling in China , presenting to the world a China that is friendly , more technologically advanced , and safer than the US . This is a side of China seldom seen in mainstream US media outlets . What better means of presenting a picture of an attractive China than through the mouths of enthusiastic American TikTok influencers themselves ? <p> Second , and equally important , many American TikTok users who have opened an account on Red are angry about the proposed TikTok ban . One TikTok influencer knows how to endear herself to potential new Chinese followers . Her first video post on Red is a study in how to make friends and gain influence . If you mute the sound and simply look at what she 's doing , you 'll think she 's merely performing a three-minute make-up routine . But unmute the video and you 'll hear her " advice " : <p> " So I have officially decided that I will be taking my content over to RedNote , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ angry that our Congress refuses to do anything on climate change while California burns , and then they all engage in the conversation of who 's to blame . I 'm angry that our kids get shot in their classrooms while they play thoughts and prayers and refuse to make any progress either on gun controls or on mental health support and reforms . I am angry that they can get together and come to bipartisan agreement on banning a communication platform , but they ca n't get together and come up with any sort of bipartisan agreement on what we should be doing with our border . I am angry at the paternalistic attitude of acting as if they are going to protect us from Chinese Communist interference , when we know our own government is running all sorts of observations on China -- and American citizens -- that they are n't being transparent about ... " <p> Is Red quivering with excitement or trepidation ? Despite the enticing prospect of a massive migration of TikTok users , it ca n't be undiluted joy and triumph at Red 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the opportunities must be as seductive as the risks must be frightening . Either way , it is hard to imagine Red not wanting to turn itself into another TikTok , reproducing an arrangement that allows TikTok to coexist internationally with its domestic Chinese counterpart Douyin . <p> The arrival of thousands of TikTok refugees is a double-edged sword . The sudden flood of American users on this platform is opening up new , Western target audiences for Chinese propaganda , but those same audiences are unlikely to be as obedient and rule-abiding as their Chinese counterparts . It 's only a matter of time before Western users realise they have hit a censorship wall , and they wo n't like it . <p> Moreover , Westerners -- especially those from the US -- may happily post material that bashes America while also praising China , inadvertently presenting the ideal patriotic education material to domestic Chinese audiences . The flipside is this is also likely to present attractive and vivid images of a whole new Western world to the Chinese public -- a world that so far still manages to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some Western politicians ; a world where people can criticise the government without their posts being routinely taken down , or worse . <p> It will be fascinating to watch how things unfold in this space in the weeks to come . <p> Have something to say about this article ? @@120124804 <p> For the first time , the Moon has been added to the World Monuments Fund global " watch list " of heritage places in need of protection and preservation . <p> According to the New York-based , non-for-profit organisation , the coming era of space exploration and tourism puts cultural sites like the Apollo landing sites at risk from damage and looting . <p> " We have about 100 places on the Moon where different nations have put material , " Alice Gorman , a space archaeologist at Flinders University and one of the researchers who worked on the nomination for the list , said . <p> " It might be a crash landing . It might be a human landing site , a robotic probe or rover . " <p> The designation applies not just to those sites , butto the whole Moon , which Dr Gorman said was " really significant " . <p> " The nomination serves a few purposes , " she said . <p> " It acknowledges the severity of the threat ... it raises awareness , and it puts the international space community @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Fund watch list ? <p> First launched in 1996 , the World Monuments Fund biennial watch list aims to raise awareness of significant historic sites in need of protection . <p> The 2025 list highlighted 25 historic places facing major challenges from issues such as climate change , conflict and natural disaster . <p> Dr Gorman was part of a committee that looked at aerospace heritage for the International Council of Monuments and Sites ( ICOMOS ) , which undertook the nomination . <p> Unlike the UNESCO World Heritage listings , which need to be undertaken by a country where a site is located , the World Monuments Watch listings are picked from nominations from individuals or community-based groups anywhere in the world . <p> UNESCO 's World Heritage convention also does n't apply to space . <p> " The World Heritage convention has concepts that are really useful for us , but we ca n't actually apply the convention , " Dr Gorman said . <p> " So , this is a win for ICOMOS in terms of being able to get some good standards and principles in place @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? <p> While the team only nominated Tranquillity Base , the Apollo 11 landing site in 1969 , the final listing on the World Monuments Watch was much broader . <p> " We were very delighted when they extended that initial nomination to include the whole Moon , " Dr Gorman said . <p> Apollo landing sites as seen from the Southern Hemisphere . ( NASA/Ben Spraggon ) <p> The listing notes there are more than 90 historic sites " that mark humankind 's presence on the Moon 's surface and testify to some of our most extraordinary feats of courage and ingenuity . " <p> There 's evidence of six other Apollo missions across the Moon 's surface , and many other rovers and landers from nations around the world including the US , China , Russia and India . <p> A historic site that Dr Gorman said was regularly forgotten was the first human-made object that made contact with another celestial body . A Russian probe called Lunar Two landed on the Moon in 1959 , and detonated a ball of sodium gas on impact so it could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Bernard Lovell observed it from the Jodrell Bank Telescope in Manchester , " she said . <p> " It was the very first human contact with the Moon . " <h> What are the threats to the Moon ? <p> According to Dr Gorman , there are a number of ways that further space travel to the Moon could destroy or damage the artefacts already there . <p> " Increased traffic on the Moon could mean a lot more dust moving around , and all those amazing cultural heritage places being gradually worn away by sharp abrasive lunar dust , " she said . <p> " You do n't even have to land next to or near one for there to be an impact . " <p> Objects on the Moon are also at risk of being taken , as there is a large trade in space objects on Earth . <p> " Somebody would pay a lot of money for a piece of the Apollo 11 landing site , " Dr Gorman said . <p> Space law says no-one can lay claim to our biggest natural satellite , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ need to preserve our Moon heritage -- and time is running out . <p> While permanent settlements , tourism and lunar mining could all cause damage to heritage sites , there may be ways to limit their impacts . <p> Dr Gorman suggested an environmental impact assessment process -- similar to ones we have on Earth -- could be done in the planning stages of space missions to minimise any disruptions to important heritage areas . <p> " There have been a number of studies proposing that an environmental impact assessment process is very necessary for space , " she said . <p> " Commercial operators going to the Moon need to be held accountable to the public . @@120126095 <p> Every spring , one of the most incredible feats of animal behaviour takes place right before our eyes . <p> A tiny animal -- with a very tiny brain -- goes busily back and forth , carrying branches , feathers , grass and sometimes fur with a very specific plan in mind -- a design for a nest . <p> Birds ' nests can come in all shapes and sizes -- from the traditional cup nests to those that hang like pendulums from the branches of trees . <p> Building a nest can take hours , days , sometimes even weeks . But each design has been refined over millions of years of evolution and is specific to each species . <p> Nests are the key to the survival of birds , quite literally holding the future of their populations within them . <p> But how did nest designs become so very different ? <p> And will they change as the planet does ? <p> Our research has been looking into these questions using over 700 museum specimens . <p> The answers will help us understand how future climatic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and their occupants , will cope in a changing world . <h> Domes , pendants and cups <p> When we think of nests , the first image that usually comes to mind is a cup , a simple structure that works like a vessel to hold eggs and chicks . But with a plethora of designs in the bird world , this vessel can take many shapes . <p> Some species build enclosed nests , domed structures with a side entrance and a roof . <p> These nests are rarer than open cups but many perching birds build them , including Australian species like lyrebirds , thornbills , gerygones and fairy-wrens . Building a roof may be a tool to help protect young from higher levels of solar radiation . <p> Butcher bird and young in a flat nest . Picture : Jessica McLachlan <p> Willie wagtails build cup nests . Picture : Helberth Peixoto <p> Fairy wren young in a domed nest . Picture : Claire Taylor <p> Weaver birds build pendulum nests . Picture : Getty Images <p> 1 / 4 <p> Researchers are only just starting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ designs . There are broad architectural differences but , as with human houses , there is also variation in many other features . <p> Some nests have incredibly thick walls , while others you can see right through . Some nests are pendant shaped and elongated , while other nests are wide and flat . <p> Our team , along with others across the world , are studying why species build nests the specific ways they do , and how we ended up with such a huge variety of nest designs . <p> To do this , we looked to museums as an incredible , but often overlooked resource , that not only contain collections of animal specimens , but what they build . <p> Museums across the world , including Australia , have large collections of preserved nests , with some collected centuries ago . In cases where species have disappeared , all we have left are the structures they built . <p> For example , we found that nests constructed in locations with high levels of rain had thinner walls , while nests with thicker walls tended to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ structure and measurements of domed ( a ) and open ( b ) nests ; asterisks indicate where measurements were taken . Picture : Ecology and Evolution <p> Dr Claire Taylor measuring a nest . Picture : Supplied <p> A Paroaria nigrogenis , or masked cardinal , nest collected in 1898 and stored at the Natural History Museum in Tring , UK . Picture : Supplied <p> Silvia Colombo measuring a nest . Picture : Supplied <p> 1 / 4 <p> Our findings supported at broad scale what had been reported in a few species -- that thinner walls in wet environments would allow nests to dry much faster , so puddles do n't form inside . <p> Thicker walls on the other hand , might be able to capture and hold humidity better in dry environments , which is especially important to help eggs hatch . <p> Wind also seems to be an important force driving the evolution of certain nest features , specifically in open-cup nests . Here , we found nests had deeper cups if they were built in environments with higher wind speeds . <p> This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ roof , then strong winds can dislodge eggs and nestlings . <p> The higher walls in these nests would also protect eggs from cooling down too quickly -- eggs need consistently high temperatures of around 37 ? C to develop . <p> Other studies have also shown that the size of the nest and the amount of lining material also varies depending on the local temperature , with colder conditions favouring nests with more lining that may help keep their contents warm . <p> Our results support the idea that the link between environment and nest design is more refined than we previously suspected , and that the structures we see now are made for the local conditions where the birds are breeding . <p> The insights from our study come from very closely related species of birds called tanagers , which suggests that these design alterations could have evolved relatively recently or could even be the product of experience and learning . <h> A strict design or a general set of instructions ? <p> Our research shows that closely related species can have a large range of variations in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ happens within species and populations . <p> Do all individual birds from the same species use the exact same recipe for construction ? <p> Nests are the key to the survival of birds , quite literally holding the future of their populations within them . Video : Jessica Mclachlan <p> Looking at museum specimens , we found the individuals of some species build very uniform nests ; for example , the width of the cup or height of the dome varies by less than two per cent . <p> But there are some species that show extreme variation in the shape of nests they build , with some building both open-cup and enclosed domed nests within the same species . <p> Because similar levels of variation were found in closely related species , this nest building flexibility may be genetically determined , which could mean some groups of species may respond more effectively to global climate change . <p> It 's interesting to note that flexibility in food foraging behaviour did not appear to correlate with flexibility in nest construction . <p> Our study was a proof-of-concept that we could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but we need more research to understand why some species are much more flexible in their designs . <h> Avian architects of the future <p> Nest builders are deeply connected to their environment and their constructions tend to match their local climatic conditions . <p> We found this was the case across millions of years of evolution , but the obvious question is , what happens if we suddenly change the environments where birds are building their nests ? <p> What happens if the temperatures where they breed become much warmer ? And if the materials they build their nests with are not available anymore ? <p> While we do n't yet have these answers and more research is needed , it 's clear that these environmental changes could have dramatic consequences for bird populations . <p> For example , recent research has already told us that temperatures inside nests are rising and this is leading to a decline in some bird populations . <p> There is almost no information about if and how quickly birds can adjust their designs . Nor about how effective those changes would be in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ time to appreciate the wonder of nest building if you are lucky enough to see it happening . Picture : Pardalote/ Jessica McLachan <p> Our work suggests that not all birds will be able to adjust their designs within the tight time frames that might protect them from a warming climate , so some species might have to respond in ways that do n't involve architectural solutions , like shifting their ranges or breeding at a different time . <p> Other species might be able to adjust specific design features to decrease temperatures inside their nests or use different types of materials that can offer better insulation . <p> Next spring , spare some time to appreciate the wonder of nest building if you are lucky enough to see it happening . <p> The designs that have evolved over millions of years may not stay the same , needing adjustments to cope with the challenges imposed by humanity . <h> Follow Pursuit <p> Social media <h> Acknowledgement of country <p> We acknowledge Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as the Traditional Owners of the unceded lands on which we work @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ past , present and future , and acknowledge the importance of Indigenous knowledge in the Academy . 
@@120150119 <h> Tackling urban heat with Greater Sydney Heat Smart City Plan <p> The threat of extreme heat is growing , climate change is making heatwaves more frequent , intense , and long-lasting . These heatwaves are now recognised as Australia 's deadliest natural hazard , causing more deaths than bushfires , storms , or floods . <p> To address this , the Greater Sydney Heat Smart City Plan has been launched , offering a clear strategy to protect people , infrastructure , and the environment from rising temperatures . <p> Heatwaves can cause serious health problems , including increased hospital admissions , and also impact the economy by reducing productivity . They strain vital services like energy and water supplies . <p> Western Sydney is especially at risk . By 2090 , it could face 20 more days a year where temperatures exceed 35 ? C , triple the number experienced today . This alarming projection makes it clear that action is urgently needed to manage the growing threat of heat . <p> Launched on 5 December , the Heat Smart City Plan is a five-year initiative to make Greater @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with input from over 40 organisations and nearly 400 individuals , including experts from health , environment , urban planning , business , government , and community groups . This teamwork ensures the plan addresses the needs of the entire city . <p> The Plan builds on earlier work to protect vulnerable areas like Western Sydney and focuses on practical steps to keep communities safe during heatwaves . <p> The Plan emphasises cooling urban areas by expanding tree coverage and adding more green spaces , such as rooftop gardens and shaded areas , to help lower temperatures . <p> It also prioritises the use of heat-resistant materials in roads and buildings while incorporating shaded structures in public spaces to reduce heat stress . <p> Protecting people is another key focus , with measures such as setting up cooling centres and developing community programmes to support vulnerable groups like the elderly and those with health issues during heatwaves . <p> Technology plays a central role , with heat hotspots being monitored across the city to assess the effectiveness of cooling projects and ensure resources are used efficiently . <p> The Plan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ensuring that it aligns with existing policies and maximises its overall impact . <p> Image : Greater heat resilience for Greater Sydney / NSW Government <h> You May Also Like : <h> Discover new products <p> Discover products that suit your style and create a list of the items you like or want most . 
@@120150121 <p> ' Future Climate Future Home ' is all about engage current experts and the next generation of designers and planners with climate-sensitive urban design techniques . <p> Commentary on climate change is often alarmist and can employ inflammatory language . <p> Words like ' catastrophe ' , ' threat ' and ' urgency ' are widely used . The problem is that such commentary can lead to denial , paralysis , apathy , or even perverse reactive behaviour . <p> At the same time , a major blockage to transformational change is a lack of design vision that can capture the public imagination for more sustainable and climate-adapted futures . <p> With this in mind , the Australian Urban Design Research Centre and University of Western Australia School of Design 's latest design competition , ' Future Climate Future Home , ' aims to engage current experts and the next generation of designers and planners with climate-sensitive urban design techniques and elicit innovative climate-sensitive urban design solutions . <p> This international ideas competition is open to tertiary students and graduates from any climate region worldwide .

Exceptionally hot and dry conditions turned forests and grasslands into fuel , priming the landscape to burn . So when Santa Ana winds gusting up to 161 kilometres an hour roared off the southern California deserts , the suburbs of LA ignited and burnt all the way to the Pacific coast . During winter . It 's a textbook example of what we can expect as fossil fuel-induced warming continues to ravage our planet . New analysis based on temperature datasets generated by key scientific agencies around the world showed that 2024 was approximately 1.55 degrees above pre-industrial levels recorded since 1850 . Significantly , 2024 is the first year the global temperature has exceeded the Paris Agreement 's goal of 1.5 degrees -- it 's an unmistakable sign of the deep trouble we are in . Global greenhouse gas concentrations reached record highs last year , with no clear decline in sight . In fact , methane -- a powerful heat-trapping gas that is about 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide in the near term -- has risen sharply , worrying scientists because of its instrumental role in triggering periods of abrupt climate change . Ocean temperatures reached record highs in 2024 , driven by an El Ni ? o event that peaked in December 2023 . Because warm water evaporates more easily , elevated ocean temperatures led to a record-breaking amount of water in the atmosphere last year . The system used to comprise a large number of asylum seekers who had arrived by boat , but now the majority are individuals whose visas have been cancelled on character grounds . @@120165038 <h> Sydney Festival a mishmash of hits and misses <p> Originally conceived to attract residents into the city centre during the first month of the year , the Sydney Festival began in 1977 . At the time , people were sceptical . There was doubt about whether Sydney could produce an arts festival of real cultural merit . In the 48 years since , the festival has pursued that endeavour with varying results . <p> Stephen " Festival " Hall , a former artistic director of The Australian Opera ( now Opera Australia ) , was the founding festival director . There have been eight festival directors since , including , most recently , acclaimed theatre-makers Wesley Enoch and Lindy Hume and Belgian curator Lieven Bertels . The 2025 season is the fourth curated by Olivia Ansell , previously head of contemporary performance at the Sydney Opera House . It is also her last . What is the state of the festival now ? It 's hard to say . <p> Hall 's focus on free events , open space activation and partnerships with arts companies both locally and abroad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ him transform the event into an annual milestone . And it was those free events and free spaces , places where you could construct moments and exchange ideas between performances and events , that lit up past festivals . <p> Ansell 's seasons seem to have lacked that vital connective tissue , with her tenure coming amid recovery from the Covid-19 lockdowns , political tensions and protests over funding sources , and a growing cost-of-living crisis . Free performances are harder to come by in this tougher , more budget-conscious era , and festival spaces do n't always feel welcoming for lingering audience members to gather , art-adjacent , and find community . <p> Typically , these opening weekend shows would be thought of as tone-setting , an idea of what we can expect during the month . Yet the focus dropped and split quickly thereafter . <p> The Thirsty Mile precinct features overpriced drinks and snacks in rooms that feel conspicuously empty whenever I drop by , outside the opening night party , which was stacked with invited guests . Without the opportunity to linger and be immersed in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australia is in a funding crisis , and when these events are diminished , so too is our engagement . <p> The festival 's opening week of theatre , like so many opening weeks before it , is a product of its time , its conditions and the city that holds it . Can we embrace something that feels so disparate and disconnected ? <p> We began with provocations . @@120188579 <p> Van Doren and collaborators used machine learning to process and analyse 18,300 hours of acoustic recordings of autumn nocturnal bird migrations from over 26 sites in eastern North America . They detected the signature flight calls of 27 species , including 25 well-sampled songbirds . <p> The team measured how often different species ' calls could be heard together in the same recording -- testing 15 , 30 , and 60 second intervals -- and found stronger associations between species than expected by chance alone . <p> These social associations were stronger among species with similar wing size and calls . <p> " Species with similar wing sizes were more likely to associate , and wing length is directly linked to flight speed , " Van Doren says . " If you imagine 2 species flying at similar speeds because they have similar wings , then it 's much easier for them to stick together . <p> " As for vocalisations , it is possible that species ' calls have converged over time because of this social link or that species that happen to give similar calls are simply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Last year , the co-authors found that birds across northeastern North America " buddy up " with other species at stopover sites during migration . Their new findings suggest that social relationships between songbird species are also important during migratory flights . <p> " We ca n't be sure what they 're saying , but birds might broadcast calls during flight to signal their species , age , and sex . And we can certainly speculate that these flight calls could relate to navigation or finding suitable stopover habitat , " says Van Doren . <p> They speculate that short-lived songbird species , which do not learn their migration routes from their parents , may rely on social ties with other species alongside innate patterning and memory to make the journey . As climate change and habitat loss causes declines in bird biodiversity , this may jeopardise co-migrating partner species in unknown ways . <p> " Learning more about the consequences of these social connections -- not only for migration , but also for other aspects of their biology -- will be important to inform and manage the risks they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> To better understand these dynamics , the team now plans to attach tiny microphones to individual birds to track their " conversations " throughout migration . 
@@120188580 <p> Conservation managers recognise the need for new ways to help species and ecosystems adapt to climate change . But dreaming up new tactics and testing them out requires lots of time , effort and -- often -- money . <p> So we decided to gather examples of new tactics from Australia and around the world and offer them up in one place . Our free new online tool is full of fresh ideas to help Australian conservation groups find out about what might be worth trying on their patch . <p> The catalogue contains more than 400 interventions such as purpose-built shelters and cooling systems , or relocation programs moving species to areas where the future climate may be more suitable . Having a ready-made toolkit means we can respond more rapidly and effectively to the changing environment , helping preserve Australia 's unique biodiversity . <h> Replacing lost habitat : from cod logs to frog bogs <p> Our project team searched through academic papers , reports and plans , and connected with dozens of different organisations undertaking climate change adaptation in Australia . <p> We found many new @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change . We fed this information into the new Adaptation Catalogue for Conservation we call " AdaptLog " -- a searchable public repository of conservation interventions for climate adaptation . We also invited conservation groups to add to the database . <p> These logs are made from local , hollowed-out timber . They are then placed in the river to provide shelter and nesting habitat for the endangered Mary River cod . <p> Early results have been encouraging , with researchers monitoring large male cod using the logs as nesting sites , protecting their brood of eggs . <p> Tailor-made frog habitat is being recreated after fires , or during dry times . <p> More than half of East Gippsland in Victoria burned during the 2019 -- 20 Black Summer Bushfires , forcing many frogs into urban areas . In response , the East Gippsland Catchment Management Authority urged people to build temporary habitats for frogs in their backyards . <p> A " frog hotel " can be built using a large container or pot , soil , native plants and PVC pipes . They allow frogs to take refuge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ protection from predators such as kookaburras , dogs and cats . <p> Frog hotels come in many shapes and sizes . East Gippsland Catchment Management Authority <p> The West Gippsland Catchment Management Authority worked with the conservation group Greening Australia to create another type of tailor-made frog habitat they call " frog bogs " . Frog bogs look deceptively simple , just like ordinary farm dams , but they contain multiple chambers at various depths , allowing tadpoles to grow , shelter and safely feed . Native vegetation is planted around the edges , water plants are added and rocks allows frogs to bask . <p> Many groups around Australia are testing atmospheric cooling systems for keeping heat-sensitive flying foxes cool after mass deaths during heatwaves . One of these trials , jointly funded by WWF-Australia , the City of Greater Bendigo and the Department of Environment , Land , Water and Planning , was a success in Bendigo 's Rosalind Park . Hundreds of flying foxes had died in a record-breaking heatwave in the previous year , but despite temperatures climbing above 40 ? C during the trial , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ testing and are a far cry from the scale needed to support functioning ecosystems and populations . But it is heartening to see lots of passionate people working so hard to support nature in these challenging times . <p> The Turtle Cooling Project -- a partnership between WWF-Australia , The University of Queensland and the Conflict Islands Conservation Initiative , with funding support from furniture company Koala -- tested ways to cool turtle nests on the beach , so more males would hatch . Further testing promises to identify which beaches need these interventions most , and how communities can get involved around Australia and the world . <h> Sharing is caring <p> By sharing these strategies , we can help conservation managers act quickly and decisively , drawing on evidence of what has worked elsewhere . We can also provide more opportunities for communities to get involved as volunteers helping out with different kinds of adaptation actions . <p> Conservation managers in Australia and globally can now use this tool to share and find new ideas . They can also add more examples and tactics to the tool , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ settings . <p> It is very early days for this field of climate adaptation research and practice , so there is still a long way to go to build an evidence base . But by collating what is happening already , we hope to encourage the development and dissemination of more innovative approaches to give wildlife a fighting chance . <p> We would like to acknowledge the following people for their contributions to the development of AdaptLog : Jason Hartog , Alistair Hobday , Sarah Boulter , Ingrid van Putten , Jenny Styger , the Project 2.7 Steering Committee , AdaptLog beta testers and CS2.7 case study participants . @@120199513 <p> So , how has public opinion shifted ? First , there is a consensus that climate change is happening and that we should respond . Both main parties already support the 2050 net zero target . <p> Second , we should transition away from coal generation as the current fleet of generators reaches the end of their economic lives . Only a fringe view still argues for building new coal-generation capacity . <p> Third , given our natural advantages in renewables ( solar and wind ) , these should form the core of the replacement capacity . The daily fluctuations in renewables generation should be smoothed with batteries and pumped hydro . <p> Fourth : renewables , by themselves , can not provide assured reliability . In sustained periods of low renewable generation , additional generation capacity will be needed . This additional capacity will also be needed during the lumpy phase-out of coal generation . <p> Will electricity be cheaper for households ? Probably not . <p> Fifth : community concerns about the safety of nuclear have diminished . The unresolved issues are cost and speed of implementation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ longer term , nuclear may well play a role , although its practical implementation here is at least twenty years away -- longer than the economic lifetime of the current coal-generation fleet . <p> Sixth : this gap will be filled by gas generation . Climate transition will not be possible without a key role for gas -- recognised in Labor 's 2024 Future Gas Strategy , which sees a role for gas even beyond 2050 . <p> Advertisement <p> Of course , there is no absolute unanimity on these issues -- just an emerging consensus with plenty of dissenting voices and loud vested interests . But it is the basis of a sensible path forward , supported by a majority of public opinion . <p> Under such a strategy , we would press forward with the expansion of renewables ( and their grid connections and battery support ) , knowing that in any longer-term mix of generation , renewables capacity should be substantially larger than at present . <p> Gas generation capacity should be installed in time to cover the coal generation transition over the next decade and , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ generation of renewables . <p> Assuring adequate gas supply will require more support from state governments ( Victoria has already accepted this change ) , building LNG facilities , and negotiating supply agreements with Australian LNG producers , who will recognise such agreements as being in their long-term interests . <p> Meanwhile , we should begin the decades-long process of exploring the nuclear option . The first few years will be taken up with revising the federal and state legislation which currently prohibits any nuclear development . <p> This period will be politically fraught but economically low-cost and without firm commitment . This gives time to explore the practical issues of construction and cost before commitment . <p> Loading <p> Experience shows a five-fold difference in cost between the Korean-built turnkey nuclear reactors in the UAE , on the one hand , and the cost and time overrun disasters of Hinkley Point in the UK and Vogtle in the US , on the other . <p> Over the next few years , we can assess where we might be on this cost spectrum , depending on our state capacity , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and specialised technical knowledge . We benefit from evolving overseas experience , including with small modular reactors , not yet in commercial operation . <p> Nuclear is ranked among the hardest of the big project challenges , and success requires comprehensive pre-planning rather than a race against the clock to fill the gap left by the retirement of coal generation . The next decade will clarify many of the current uncertainties about the long-term mix of technology . <p> How will Australia 's substantial rooftop capacity fit with other modes of generation , with its surplus of essentially free energy during the daytime ? What happens to battery and storage technology , including EV-to-grid ? What are the opportunities to shift electricity demand over the course of the day to benefit from cheap electricity ? Other details will fall into place , such as the timetable of economic phasing-out of coal generation . <p> Will electricity be cheaper for households ? Probably not . " <h> The Australian bushfire <p> For this story , we 'll look at a typical bushfire under different conditions according to the Australian Fire Danger Rating System ( AFDRS ) . ( ABC News : Alex Lim ) <p> 1 . Heat draws turbulent air , moisture and smoke up into the atmosphere . <p> 2 . @@120199805 <p> The Australian War Memorial , rightly regarded as one of the world 's finest institutions of its kind , movingly commemorates the experiences of Australians in war . And the Museum of Australian Democracy at Old Parliament House vividly conveys the history of our political system . <p> Yet , for a country whose leaders often declare that we " punch above our weight " on the global stage , there is no institution dedicated to celebrating or explaining Australia 's foreign policy and diplomatic achievements . <p> This is an oversight that Canberra , as the political capital , is uniquely positioned to correct . <p> Diplomacy is a vital part of the Australian story . Picture Shutterstock <p> Diplomacy is a vital part of the Australian story - one that deserves to be showcased in its own right . Foreign policy is about more than treaties and summits . <p> It is about how we define and protect our national interests in a complex and ever-changing world . It is the story of Australians who have navigated crises , forged partnerships , and shaped international norms in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the globe . <p> Consider , for instance , Australia 's role in the founding of the United Nations , where Doc Evatt championed the rights of smaller nations . Reflect on our leadership in the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation ( APEC ) forum , the Cairns Group on trade , or our peacekeeping efforts in places like Timor Leste and Solomon Islands . <p> These are milestones in a national journey that has balanced pragmatic realism with a commitment to the rules-based international order . <p> While the Australian War Memorial rightly focuses on the lived experiences of soldiers in combat , it leaves relatively little room to explore the broader strategic and diplomatic decisions that defined Australia 's involvement in conflicts or our efforts to secure peace . <p> How , for instance , did Australia calculate its national interests in World War II , the Cold War , or the post-9/11 era ? <p> What lessons can we learn from our engagement with the Asia-Pacific region or our responses at the international level to global challenges like climate change and pandemics ? <p> A museum of Australian diplomacy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ education and debate on the country 's place in the world . <p> Such a museum could serve multiple purposes . It would celebrate our diplomatic successes , honour the individuals who have advanced Australia 's interests abroad , and explore the difficult decisions and missteps that are an inevitable part of any nation 's foreign policy history . <p> Interactive exhibits could bring to life the high-stakes negotiations of the past , while immersive displays might simulate modern-day challenges like international trade talks or multilateral climate negotiations . <p> Crucially , a museum of diplomacy would also provide a platform to consider the future . As the Indo-Pacific becomes increasingly contested , Australia 's policymakers face difficult choices about how to balance relationships with the United States and China , engage with south-east Asia , and address emerging threats like cyber attacks and disinformation . <p> A museum could help Australians understand the complexities of these decisions , fostering a more informed and engaged public . <p> Diplomacy is often described as " the art of the possible , " but it is also an investment in our shared @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is waning and misinformation threatens to erode democratic discourse , a museum of Australian diplomacy could serve as a reminder of what can be achieved through patience , compromise , and dialogue . <p> Moreover , such an institution would complement Canberra 's existing cultural landscape . It could draw on the archives of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade ( DFAT ) , showcasing artifacts , correspondence , and photographs that tell the story of Australia 's engagement with the world . It could collaborate with universities and think tanks to host lectures , workshops , and exhibitions , becoming a hub for students , researchers , and the broader public . <p> The museum would also offer an opportunity to highlight the contributions of diverse Australians to foreign policy . From Indigenous leaders who have fostered cultural diplomacy to women who broke barriers in international negotiations , these stories deserve to be told and celebrated . <p> By doing so , the museum could inspire the next generation of Australians to see diplomacy as a calling , not just a career . <p> The establishment of a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but the returns would be significant . In addition to enhancing Canberra 's status as a destination for international visitors , it would enrich the understanding of Australians about the nation 's foreign policy priorities and a recognition that the decisions we make today will shape the legacy we leave for future generations . <p> A museum of Australian diplomacy would not only fill a gap in the city 's cultural offerings but , above all , affirm our commitment to navigating an increasingly complex world with wisdom and resolve . <p> Bryce Wakefield is the chief executive officer of the Australian Institute of International Affairs .
