@@120232212 <p> Two weeks into 2025 and it already feels like a turning point for climate action -- for good and bad . We start the year with news that the Earth experienced yet another ' warmest year on record ' and global temperatures surpassed the 1.5-degree mark for the first time . Los Angeles is on fire in the middle of winter , and Donald Trump is returning as US President . <p> The task ahead of us -- phasing out the use of fossil fuels , investing in clean energy technologies , and protecting vulnerable communities from the locked-in impacts of climate change -- remains huge . <p> But the task is not insurmountable and there are reasons for optimism that fossil fuel companies will be held legally and financially responsible for the damages caused by climate change , thanks to progress in the field of climate attribution science . <h> Bridging the gap between polluters and legal liability <p> I recently attended the Attribution Science and Climate Law Conference in New York , hosted by Columbia University 's Sabin Center for Climate Change Law ( recordings of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ channel ) . It was a deeply enlightening conference that generated significant optimism among climate scientists and lawyers alike around potential applications in climate litigation . <p> The conference served as a strong demonstration of the progress that is being made in the field of climate attribution science , which promises to deepen our ability to quantify and attribute the climate change-related damages for which individual companies , countries , and fossil fuel projects should be held responsible . <p> Climate attribution science is not a particularly new field . It is the field of science that -- using real-world observations and climate models -- established the link between a surge in anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions , starting from the Industrial Revolution , and the observed increases in global temperatures and changes in the Earth 's climate patterns . <p> Attribution science works to confirm the linkages between five core components of the causes and effects of climate change , these being : <p> -- The damage attributable to changes in climate and weather patterns ( property damage , displacement , social and cultural loss ) . <p> At the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of fossil fuels . At the other end of the chain are the economic , social , cultural , and ecological damages caused by climate change . <p> Establishing the links across the full attribution chain with sufficient certainty and higher levels of specificity is often one of the hardest aspects of climate science . We often hear claims that it is impossible to attribute an individual extreme weather event to climate change or the individual contributions of a fossil fuel project to global warming . <p> But the increasing sophistication of the field promises to bridge any gaps or uncertainties that may remain in the attribution chain with amazing levels of specificity -- we are reaching the point of assessing the impacts of emissions from individual countries , individual fossil fuel companies and even individual emitters . <p> For example , speaking at the Sabin Center 's conference , researchers from the National Bureau of Economic Research demonstrated how it could be used to determine how just one year of private jet usage by Elon Musk would be responsible for more than $1 million worth of cumulative climate change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ growing sophistication of climate science that responsibility for climate damages will be able to be quantified on the basis of individual countries and regions . It could enable young people to sue fossil fuel companies for future climate impacts , and it could provide the evidentiary basis for countries , like small island states in the Pacific , to seek compensation from major fossil fuel producing countries , like Australia . <h> Simplifying the complexity of climate accountability <p> The global climate system is large and complex , and the large number of carbon polluters means each argues they individually contribute only a ' small ' and ' trivial ' share of the observed increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations . The ' drop in the ocean ' argument . <p> But , as we know , the aggregation of all those ' small ' sources of pollution adds up to the unprecedented release of carbon and is resulting in measurable changes to the global climate . <p> Demonstrating the causal link between an individual fossil fuel producer and the damage caused by climate change is also one of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ claims for legal intervention or financial compensation if the link between a cause and the resulting damage is considered too uncertain , or the contribution of the defendant appears too trivial . <p> For example , in the Sharma appeal ( also known as the ' duty of care ' case ) , the Full Federal Court ruled the federal environment minister did not owe young people a duty of care to protect them from climate change in part because of the " the tiny contribution of the minister 's coal mine approval to the overall risk of harm ... the intermediation of countless other people around the world and the indeterminacy of the liability . " <p> But the number of polluters is n't actually that large -- a landmark study published by Richard Heede in 2013 identified a list of the ' carbon majors ' . A recent update to Heede 's study finds that 70 per cent of historical greenhouse gas emissions can be attributed to " just 78 corporate and state producing entities " -- including Australia 's BHP , which is responsible for around 0.5% @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that their individual contributions are trivial , these ' carbon majors ' seek to undermine any argument that they should be held responsible for the resulting damage caused by climate change . But as climate attribution science is increasingly able to demonstrate , while the individual contributions may sound trivial , the causal links can be readily demonstrated and the resulting damages are anything but trivial . <p> This would put BHP 's proportional liability for the economic damages caused by climate change at somewhere around US$200 billion annually , or about 60% more than its current market capitalisation . Science will soon be able to pin responsibility for damages on an individual company like BHP , and potentially enable impacted communities to sue for compensation . <h> A tool to reveal the impact of proposed fossil fuel projects <p> Another opportunity created by climate attribution science is the potential to quantify the future climate damage of proposed fossil fuel projects . <p> These arguments , unfortunately , are too often swallowed and regurgitated by regulators . This includes the current federal environment minister Tanya Plibersek , who sought to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Mount Pleasant coal mine , when approving the project under the EPBC Act . <p> " I found that the amount of coal to be combusted from the proposed action , and the possible increase in net global GHG emissions and global average temperature that would result from combusting this amount of coal , are very small . I concluded that the proposed action would not be a ' substantial ' cause of the physical effects of climate change on World Heritage properties . " <p> -- Federal Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek <p> But in the context of massive potential economic damages -- returning to that $38 billion figure -- a rough estimate the proportional share of economic climate damages attributable to the Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion results in a figure that is no longer trivial . The share of climate change damages for which the expansion would be responsible could be as much as $4.5 billion annually . <p> The growing sophistication of climate attribution science will allow more detailed and more accurate assessments of the future economic damages that may be caused by a proposed project in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ such damages -- and the climate change significance of individual projects -- are not trivial and , crucially , not acceptable under environment and planning laws . <p> This article was originally published by Tempests &amp; Terawatts . @@120258330 <h> Most people in most countries trust scientists , especially Australia <p> A big global survey has revealed people want scientists to be more involved in the policy-making process of most governments . <p> The survey , of nearly 72,000 people in 68 countries , has found that most people have a high trust in science . <p> The study , which is published today in Nature Human Behaviour , found no evidence for a widespread lack of trust in science . <p> " Counter to narratives of a ' crisis of trust ' in science , our findings reveal most people worldwide have relatively high trust in scientists and want them to be more involved in society and policymaking , " says co-author Dr Mathew Marques , a senior lecturer at La Trobe University . <p> Australians were the 5th most trusting in science in the world , after Egypt , India , Nigeria and Kenya . <p> The team of 241 researchers ran an online survey of 71,922 people from 2022-2023 . The survey was a questionnaire asking respondents to rate how much they agreed with various statements @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the policymaking process " . <p> The researchers also collected information on demographics , education , political orientation and religiosity . <p> Associate Professor Fabien Medvecky , from the Australian National University , who was n't involved in the research , says it 's " probably the broadest and most robust work he 's seen that addresses the issue of trust in science , and especially trust in scientists across the globe " . <p> The study found that no country had low levels of trust in science . <p> " More interesting is that many of the stories we hear about leads to ( dis ) trust are challenged when we take a broader , more robust look , " says Medvecky . <p> There were variations within and between countries on scientific trust . <p> Political orientation affected trust in some countries , but the effect differed from place to place . North American and Western European countries showed a link between conservatism and lack of trust in science , while some Eastern European , Southeast Asian and African countries , saw a link between right-leaning politics and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and right-left , political orientations separately . ) <p> " The attitudes of political leadership rather than peoples ' political orientation may better explain politically correlated attitudes towards scientists , " write the researchers in their paper . <p> " Unlike North America and many Western European countries , in Australia having a conservative versus liberal political orientation was not associated with trust , " says Marques . <p> " This could mean political polarisation around science is not as much of an issue as it is for specific scientific issues , like climate change . " <p> Overall , there was a positive link between religiosity and science : that is , people with strong religious beliefs were more likely to have a higher trust in science . <p> This relationship also varied between countries . The researchers found a strong link between trust and religiosity in Muslim-majority countries like T ? rkiye , Bangladesh , and Malaysia , while the relationship was varied and sometimes negative in Christian-majority countries . <p> The researchers found only a small positive link between tertiary education and trust in science , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Too often we see a headline that says the community does not trust science . @@120272178 <p> Executive orders can also play an important role in laying out major policy agendas . <p> While these orders are legally binding , they are not legislation as they do n't require approval from Congress . <p> It does n't necessarily mean the president can enact orders without challenge , as Congress could still block an order from being fulfilled by removing funding or creating other hurdles . <p> Only a sitting US president can overturn an existing executive order . <p> New presidents will often issue orders to cancel the orders of their predecessors . <p> Other presidential documents -- such as proclamations and political memorandums -- can also be similar to executive orders , but have different purposes . <p> However , all three are used by presidents to pursue actions they ca n't get through Congress . <h> What are the limitations to executive orders ? Throughout the elections of the past year , citizens have raised their voices against business , government , and the wealthy across the globe . Incumbent parties have been ousted in Western democracies , including the US , UK , France , Germany and Canada . Business has been pushed back on for its involvement in societal issues , from DEI to sustainability . <p> " Grievance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ business and government make things worse , and the rich keep getting richer . @@120317162 <p> A new study has found most respondents trust scientists and agree that scientists should engage more in society , also warning that vocal distrust even among a small minority may affect policymaking . <p> The paper , involving researchers from the Australian National University ( ANU ) and La Trobe University among 242 academics , was published in the journalNature Human Behaviour this week . <p> ANU 's Zoe Leviston said the survey indicated about two-thirds of Aussies said scientists should actively advocate for specific policies , and another 60% should be more involved in the policymaking process . <p> " Public trust in scientists is vital , " Leviston said . <p> " It can help us with personal decision making on matters like health and provide evidence-based policymaking to assist governments with crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic or climate change . " <p> The survey of 71,00 people from 68 countries reported no nation with a low trust score towards scientists . <p> Participants were asked to rank their views on a scale of 1 ( strongly disagree ) to 5 ( strongly agree ) about @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Researchers then used the responses to measure so-called " established dimensions of trustworthiness " including perceived competence , benevolence , integrity and openness . <p> Of the survey 's Australian participants , 68% either agreed or strongly agreed that scientists should communicate their findings to politicians . <p> A total of 80% of Australians said scientists have a responsibility to communicate about science with the general public . <p> " Globally , 78% of respondents perceive scientists to be qualified , while 57% perceive scientists to be honest , " Leviston added . <p> The survey further found most people worldwide , except for African and Asian countries , considered scientists were prioritising developing defence and military technologies more than they should be . <p> The relationship between people 's political views and their trust in scientists was also analysed . @@120345209 <p> Through the smoke-hazed backdrafts of the worldwide megafires lighting up the climate emergency , we can see the scorched earth of another global crisis : information collapse . <p> From Australia 's megafires in 2019-20 , to Siberia 's burning permafrost in 2020-21 , to the Mediterranean alight , particularly in Greece , in 2023 , and now to this year 's shocking winter burning of Los Angeles , each has been marked by a dramatic escalation of fake news and misinformation . <p> Each time , the key drivers of the misinformation crisis are the same : right-wing media like our own News Corp , populist politicians eager for the viral hit , and bots and trolls on social media -- often amplified by authoritarian states . <p> It 's a fakery made of part lies , part out-of-context bullshit , part deliberate falsehoods , part carelessness about truth . Welcome to what Lydia Polgreen identified in 2019 : information collapse -- the dizzying unknowability of what 's right and what 's wrong . <p> During our bushfires , Australian norms and institutions of trust -- emergency services @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ premiers -- were strong enough , just , to resist the early crumbling of the solidity of truth . <p> In California at the moment , the fake news is visibly worse , hypercharged by AI manipulation -- like the iconic Hollywood sign alight -- or adaptations of images from past fires . They 're often fact-checked on news media ( and by California Governor Gavin Newsom ) but left to roam largely unchecked on the far more powerful social platforms . <p> Even more damaging are the political untruths , fed as they now are from President Donald Trump in his inaugural address and reported more or less straight by a freshly cowed legacy media . Compare this to the robust push-back against the lamentable ( but oddly unlamented ) Craig Kelly during Australia 's megafires . <p> And there 's a new player : the big tech broligarchy ( a word we needed , courtesy of misinformation journalist Natalia Antelava ) . Following Elon Musk 's takeover , the platform that was once Twitter has been transformed into the organising and propaganda voice of the hard right ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's amplifications and running commentary . <p> Through the financial wizardry of Wall Street , Trump has become a broligarch himself , with the float of his personal microphone , Truth Social , while leading venture capitalist Marc Andreessen has become the thought leader of the anti-censorship brigade . <p> The broligarchs ( and their stenographers in right-wing media ) have weaponised " freedom of speech " as a value that overrides truth , that renders as censorship journalistic " respect for the truth " ( as Australia 's journalistic code of ethics puts it ) . <p> Post-election , Meta 's Mark Zuckerberg has fallen into line , humbling himself with an apologetic abandoning ( in the US , at least ) of content moderation on Facebook and Instagram . He 's reshaping , too , the company 's internal diversity programs to pander to the right with an avowed more " masculine " energy . <p> The new Silicon Valley right has flipped " shame " in political discourse from the red-faced embarrassment of being caught making shit up to the red-pilled shame of being , gasp , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by Musk 's cry of " shame " at German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier for his criticism of the country 's rising neo-fascist party , Alternative for Germany , as " fearmongers " over immigration . <p> Misinformation around disasters like megafires comes with a plan to advance the right 's agenda : strengthen misogyny by opposing diversity and equity ( the LA fire chief is a woman and gay ) ; dismantle public institutions with fake-news attacks on ( the Democrat-run ) state and city 's preparation and response to the fires , particularly with misleading information about California 's water policies ; and promote climate change denialism . <p> Back in Australia 's fire summer of 2019 , it was right-wing legacy media News Corp that led attempts to divert attention with twin attacks on wokesters and deviants . The blame fell on greenies for blocking backburning that would have prevented the fires , denied by both firefighters and environmentalists alike . Still , fake news never completely dies : the backburning trope has long been on high rotation in Trump 's criticism of California 's land management . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ focus to social deviancy with claims of arson , their reporting widely amplified through the favoured tool of climate denial -- bots and trolls on social media -- alongside the hashtag #Arsonemergency , designed to crowd out the previously trending #climateemergency . <p> In those more innocent days , the shame of falsehood still mattered . The strength of Australia 's network of independent media , fact-checkers and the public broadcaster , coupled with robust denials from police and firefighters , meant the story dropped out of public gaze . It drove the big break in the Murdoch family , with James Murdoch publicly criticising the Australian mastheads and subsequently resigning from the News Corp board <p> But the hunt for appropriate villains continues . When megafires broke out in Greece in 2023 , right-wing activists and the conservative government focused on their favourite target -- immigrants -- with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis saying : " It is also almost certain that this fire was started on routes that are often used by illegal migrants who have entered our country . " <p> In the US , there 's a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ For example , public radio and not-for-profit digital news in California , LAist and CalMatters , are filling the gap with a Wildfire Updates newsletter . <p> The crisis demands a new fact-based language : beginning as journalistic hyperbole , the now all-too-frequent term " megafires " has been identified in an Australian literature review as any fire burning more than 10,000 hectares . <p> Australia got through the misinformation challenge in 2019 . With the accelerating information collapse , what will happen in the all-but-inevitable next fires ? <p> Have something to say about this article ? Write to us at letters@crikey.com.au . @@120357384 <h> What made David Lynch such an influential director was his ability to create eerily universal cinematic imagery that tapped into our dreams and nightmares . By Christos Tsiolkas . <h> Remembering David Lynch , master of the uncanny <p> David Lynch , who died on January 15 , is one of the greatest and most influential directors to date . Even those perturbed or put off by his unsettling surrealist visions ca n't deny how steeped contemporary culture is in the visual and sonic grammars he created in his films and in his pioneering television masterpiece , Twin Peaks . <p> I always thought of Lynch as the first truly post-punk film director . I was a callow youth when I saw his first feature , Eraserhead ( 1977 ) , as part of a retrospective screening at an arthouse cinema in Melbourne . Though I was still intellectually unformed , I recognised the borrowings from expressionist art and cinema and his indebtedness to the great German filmmaker F. ? W. Murnau . <p> There was also something else at play : Lynch 's provocative struggles to find a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Kafka . Eraserhead is most notable for the monstrous visual elements that dominate this disturbing black-and-white film . Yet at its heart , it is an anguished study of suffering , of isolation and moral distrust . Watching Eraserhead made me feel exactly as I did when I read The Double or The Castle . The film also felt akin to the new wave music I was listening to at that time , to Talking Heads and Television , and suggestive of the photography of Diane Arbus and Robert Mapplethorpe . <p> Lynch 's monsters ca n't be pacified by psychology or by ideology . He understood that there is something about evil that remains inexplicable . <p> The discordant , industrial soundtrack to Eraserhead , composed by Lynch and Alan Splet , is as alarming and sinister as the visual motifs . The other-worldly use of " In Heaven " , the song composed by Peter Ivers , is a stand-out moment -- an accentuation of the irrationality of the dreamscape and yet , unexpectedly , also a moment of reprieve . It would become a recurring motif @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the recontextualisation of a song . There 's the startling lip-sync by Dean Stockwell to Roy Orbison 's " In Dreams " in Blue Velvet ( 1986 ) and , even more powerfully , the stunning a cappella rendition of Orbison and Joe Melson 's " Crying " in Spanish by Rebekah Del Rio in Mulholland Drive ( 2001 ) . <p> These spectacular musical moments would come to influence a subsequent generation of filmmakers , such as Emerald Fennell , Wong Kar-wai and Richard Kelly -- so much so that the reimagining of a popular song will become a clich ? of 21st century cinema . <p> What is distinctive in Lynch 's work is that such disruptions of the narrative are n't mere affect but are always markers of the collapsing of the ordinary and rational world into the uncanny , into the world of dreams . Lynch is on record as saying that one of his favourite films is the children 's classic The Wizard of Oz . Just as in that film Dorothy steps through the door of her black-and-white house into the technicolour of Oz @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ guileless protagonist of Blue Velvet , Jeffrey ( Kyle MacLachlan ) , has entered a more troubling and more perverse vision of suburbia than he ever knew existed . And as we watch the lone figure onstage singing " Llorando " ( " Crying " ) in Mulholland Drive , we are suddenly aware of the hidden and terrible histories of ghosts that populate Hollywood and Los Angeles . In Lynch 's films , however , there are no ruby red slippers to carry us safely back home . In so many of them , from Blue Velvet to Inland Empire ( 2006 ) and , of course , in Twin Peaks and its cinematic prequel , Fire Walk With Me ( 1992 ) , the dream and the nightmare and the real collapse into each other . <p> The rigour and ingenuity that Lynch applied to integrating soundscape into his visual surrealism will possibly be his greatest legacy . It is there in arguably his most formally " conservative " film , the sublime gothic fable that is The Elephant Man ( 1980 ) . Lynch was also a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ defining aspects of his work is his loyalty to his collaborators , to his editor Mary Sweeney , and to the composer Angelo Badalamenti . Lynch 's vision is singular , and he is largely the sole writer and director of most of his films , but he was always generous in his praise of his crew and actors . He gave MacLachlan his start , and it was Naomi Watts 's courageous , uncompromising performance in Mulholland Drive that cemented her career in Hollywood . Nicolas Cage gave one of his greatest performances in Wild at Heart and Laura Dern , whom I first became aware of in Blue Velvet , is astonishing in the underrated Inland Empire . The film is an attempt to adhere to the temporal , spatial and sonic language of dreams . Yet Dern does n't get lost in the ambitious overreach . Like Carroll 's Alice , her performance maintains a committed dignity and lucidity that assist the audience in navigating the frightening wonderland that Lynch created . <p> Lynch was sui generis , but he was never naive . Right from his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Eastern European surrealism in his work , as well as his appreciation of film noir . As in the films of the great Czech director Vera Chytilov ? , or in Kafka 's short stories , and the best works of film noir , there is terror as well as pleasure in Lynch 's surrealism . I have friends who stay away from his work , who find his films too distressing . I understand that . Unlike Wes Anderson 's films , in which the absurd and dream-logic are tamed , Lynch was uncompromising in placing perversity at the core of his dreamscapes . The monsters that emerge in his cinema ca n't be sequestered from our own selves . It is our desires , and our repressions , that create them . <p> There is a moment in Twin Peaks that I still ca n't shake . The camera swirls around an older man and a younger woman and our perspective alternates between that of both characters . The man is experiencing an ecstatic dance of love . The woman is looking into the eyes of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remains one of the most terrifying sequences in the history of the screen . Lynch 's monsters ca n't be pacified by psychology or by ideology . He understood that there is something about evil that remains inexplicable . <p> Yet , like all great artists , his work defies neat summation . He terrified me , but in his graceful elegy The Straight Story ( 1999 ) he directed one of the great films about ageing . Richard Farnsworth is wonderful as the dying man who decides to ride a lawnmower to visit his ill , estranged brother . My father , who never attained a good grasp of English , loved that film . The dialogue is minimal . We understand the story through gesture and the positioning of the characters within the rural landscapes . The film is pure cinema , transcending the written or spoken word . The camera and the music and the soundtrack and the editing and the actors all tell the story . And the maestro in command is David Lynch . <p> We are our dreams and we are our nightmares . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . I am grateful for that , and I am also grateful that the last image I have of David Lynch is playing the great American director John Ford in Steven Spielberg 's phenomenally good The Fabelmans ( 2022 ) . There was so much affection in that portrayal , of the struggles and vicissitudes and pleasures of making filmmaking your vocation . If there is a heaven , I hope Ford and Lynch are there together , drinking their whiskies and smoking their cigars and cigarettes . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . It relies on the support of readers . In a country with a concentration of media ownership unlike anything else in the world , it is vitally important . Your subscription helps make it possible .

The latest lithium technology comes with less danger of fire than older headlines might lead you to believe . They 're capable of a deeper discharge than lead acid batteries ( you can use up to 90% of a charge per cycle without inflicting much damage ) and are much easier to maintain with a longer lifespan . They 're also significantly more expensive and sensitive to temperature . They remain inexpensive and widely available . The technology appears promising , and it could become more widely used in residential battery backup systems in the near future . <h> Nickel-cadmium batteries <p> Nickel-cadmium batteries have a high energy density with double the energy of a lead-acid battery . Nickel-cadmium batteries are very durable , expensive and work well in extreme temperatures making them a good choice for large-scale commercial and industrial projects . Cadmium is toxic and generally not appropriate for residential use . <h> Buying a backup battery system <p> In general , a solar battery bank can cost between $10,000 to $25,000 for 10 to 25 kilowatt hours of power . @@120432383 <h> The Irish potato famine originated in South America <p> Scientists might have been looking in the wrong place to find the original source of potato blight , which could prevent discovery of ways to avoid the problem . <p> Late blight of potato and tomato , was the cause of the Great Hunger , the Irish potato famine , but it remains a problem around the world . Determining where the pathogen that causes it came from originally could help discover ways that native potato plants resist the disease . <p> A new study suggests that the microorganism , Phtytophthora infestans , originated from the South American Andes Mountains , before spreading to North America and Europe . <p> P. infestans is a type of single-celled eukaryote known as an oomycete , or water mould , which destroys the leaves and edible parts of potatoes , tomatoes , and some other nightshades . Potato blight which destroyed crops , and lack of a welfare safety , led to the starvation and death of more than one million people during the Irish great famine in the 1840s . <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from Mexico or South America has divided scientists . In a new PLOS ONEstudy , researchers analysed the whole genome sequences of P. infestans and related species to determine the answer . <p> " By sequencing these genomes and accounting for evolutionary relationships and migration patterns , we show that the whole Andean region is a hot spot for speciation , or where a species splits into 2 or more distinct species , " says Jean Ristaino , professor of plant pathology at North Carolina State University in the US and corresponding author of the paper . <p> Lead author Allison Coomber , a former NC State graduate student researcher and current bioinformatics scientist at Monoceros Biosystems , adds : " Our data shows that there have been more migrations of the pathogen into and out of South America , and the migrations into and out of Mexico are small in comparison . <p> " We did find there was gene flow from the Andes to Mexico , and in reverse , because there 's a big Mexican potato breeding program and potatoes have gone into the Andean region in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ But in historic times it was the other way around . " <p> The findings add support to a South American origin of the pathogen and suggest that examining wild Andean potato species could help researchers learn more about resistance to late blight . <p> " A lot of the search for resistance to this disease has focused on a wild potato species in Mexico -- Solanum demissum -- which was used to breed resistant potato lines that were used for the past 100 years , " Ristaino says . <p> " It points out the importance of looking at the centre of origin where a host and pathogen have evolved together over thousands of years . <p> " Climate change is bringing more drought to higher Andean elevations , so we could be losing some of these potatoes before we learn if they could provide resistance to late-blight disease . Many among that large body of home owners with mortgages largely or fully repaid are unfazed by recent concerns . Yet even within this cohort some will be hosting adult children pushed back to the family home by unaffordable rents . <p> For highly mortgaged owners -- especially recent first home buyers -- these pressures will be all too real and direct . As Alan Kohler has persuasively argued , this is a story with roots at least a quarter of a century old , a story of mistaken policy choices and complacent policy neglect by all Australian governments but especially at the federal level . <p> Admittedly , Australia is far from alone in experiencing rising rates of housing stress , which have been building over decades . Familiar benchmark nations such as the United Kingdom , the United States and Canada have been battling similar issues of declining housing affordability and rising homelessness . Even in countries such as the Netherlands , historically well-reputed on housing policy , acute pressures are nowadays @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ our own country , housing is a wickedly complex policy area made even more challenging by the division of relevant powers across the federal and state divide . That said , however , it is a sad fact that few federal administrations since the 1990s have even attempted to address Australia 's housing policy challenges in any comprehensive way . <p> All of that said , however , it is a sad fact that few federal administrations since the 1990s have even attempted to address Australia 's housing policy challenges in any comprehensive way . Despite holding crucially influential housing powers , through control over property taxation , financial regulation , social security and migration , Coalition governments have uniformly shied away from any responsibility for national housing policy leadership . <p> The Rudd and Albanese governments have attempted to interrupt this status @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I was among a group of 117 senior academics and housing industry figures who signed an open letter calling for a national housing and homelessness plan , embedded in law . <p> Proponents acknowledged the potentially useful contribution that may eventuate from the non-statutory national plan already pledged by the Albanese government , an endeavour that currently remains in development . However , we argued that underpinning legislation could entrench and build upon the advances in national housing policy leadership already achieved under the current government . <p> Drawing inspiration from equivalent 2019 Canadian legislation , a private member 's bill obliging the government of the day to develop , maintain and implement a national housing and homelessness plan was introduced into parliament by David Pocock and Kylea Tink in June 2024 . <p> The bill , which remains in the Senate in early 2025 , specifies the plan 's overarching objective as " ensuring that everyone in Australia has adequate housing " . Other consensus housing policy objectives the plan would be required to fulfil include " preventing and ending homelessness " , " improving choice in the housing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ improving housing quality " . The bill also defines accountability mechanisms . <p> Above all , it asserts the central principle that access to adequate housing is a fundamental human right affirmed in international law . Allied to this is the contention that the main priority for housing policymakers should be to facilitate population welfare not private wealth accumulation . A plan compliant with this analysis would , for example , stipulate that the prime consideration in private rental regulation should be the role of housing as a home rather than housing as an asset . <p> Advocacy for a well-founded national plan also stems from an understanding that a complex policy challenge such as housing affordability can be meaningfully addressed only by a coherent , multi-pronged , long-term strategy . It must propose actions using powers of taxation and regulation as well as expenditure . It must also recognise the need to deflate demand while maximising supply . <p> This , of course , is where things start to get controversial . It is an unfortunate irony that almost the only instance of current housing policy bipartisanship is the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ media pundits , that the prime cause of over-expensive housing is " inadequate supply " due to over-restrictive land-use planning . <p> This is a convenient position for federal politicians because it shifts blame for unaffordable housing to the state and territory governments responsible for development approval . For the current government , it is also appealing because it deflects attention from continuing timidity on winding back regressive private landlord tax breaks that encourage speculative behaviour and therefore inflate prices . <p> It also rests on a failure to recognise the reality that , as described in research for the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute , " while the planning system can create opportunities for development by zoning land and ensuring that zoning and development controls allow for a range of housing types , decisions about whether and when to develop are ultimately made by the development industry and reflect market factors " . <p> While viability limitations have been the prime cause of recently slowed construction rates , simplifying planning procedures and liberalising planning restrictions as far as possible are always worthy objectives . At the margin , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the result that future house prices and rents are slightly lower than otherwise . <p> The Albanese government 's target for construction of 1.2 million new homes by 2029 seems certain to prove a hostage to fortune , but as a vehicle to encourage planning system review by states and territories it is well-motivated . The problem is the overriding faith placed in the policy , to the exclusion of a parallel focus on demand deflation . <p> In fact , beyond the agreed case for curbing landlord tax breaks on the demand side , and modernising land-use planning systems on the supply side , there is arguably also a fair degree of consensus among housing economists and industry experts on a range of other mainstream policy reforms and initiatives needed to ease national housing woes . <p> The following list , mainly federal responsibilities but also including some state and territory issues where the Commonwealth could provide support or encouragement , is a place to start : <p> * To counter the growing exclusion of aspirant first home buyers without access to parental subsidies , there is a continuing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the government 's newly legislated Help to Buy initiative , and unlike traditionally dominant cash grants and tax breaks , these should be designed to minimise inflationary impacts and to incur minimal net expenditure . <p> * Australia should revisit mid-20th century practices of pro-first home buyer mortgage regulation and government-built homes for cost-price sale . <p> * To curb speculative behaviour that fuels inflation and to encourage more efficient use of existing housing , stamp duty should be replaced , over time , by broad-based land taxes . <p> * To enhance the experience of renting from a private provider , the Commonwealth should advocate for tenants ' rights being levelled-up to the standards of the leading jurisdictions , namely the ACT and Victoria . <p> * To expand the availability of good quality private rental housing with substantial tenure security , governments should be open to further tax and other reforms that encourage ongoing growth of build-to-rent housing -- institutionally funded apartment blocks designed for long-term rental occupancy and retained in single ownership . <p> * To reverse the damaging contraction of social and affordable housing of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extending recent investment programs such as Victoria 's Big Housing Build and the Commonwealth 's Housing Australia Future Fund . At least some of the associated costs could and should be met by the additional tax revenue from reduced private landlord tax breaks . <p> * To mitigate the impact of unaffordable rents pushing private tenants into poverty , and to remedy decades of under-indexation , further increases in Commonwealth Rent Assistance are needed . <p> To the Albanese government 's credit , actions of the past three years have already made contributions under several of these headings . As an initial phase of recovery from a decade of national neglect , this is all well and good . What remains to be revealed in Labor 's 2025 platform is whether the party recognises the need to expand , extend and transcend these initiatives . @@120444564 <h> John Hewson Labor 's soft landing is working <p> One of the main dangers of the pointscoring game that has come to define politics today is how easily it allows important policy benchmarks such as fiscal responsibility to be redefined or even jettisoned . <p> This is what we are seeing now in the Coalition 's desperation to piece together a meaningful and deliverable economic strategy . Shadow treasurer Angus Taylor has widely criticised the government 's " record " levels of spending , without proposing significant areas for cuts . Shadow finance minister Jane Hume proposes cuts to the public service to address Labor 's " big government " approach , and suggests this can be done without cuts to essential services and with no additional reliance on consultants . <p> For years the Coalition was obsessed with achieving a budget surplus . Indeed , it even got to the point of prematurely celebrating " being back in the black " , with little chance of actually achieving that . Similarly , there have been periods of obsession with government debt and now government spending . The Coalition @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ circumstances in which its calls have been made . <p> Not all debt is " bad " , nor all government spending " wasteful " . In the heady days of Tony Abbott 's government , and his National Commission of Audit to identify savings in the public sector -- driven by leading businesspeople -- I recall asking the former prime minister how he bought his house . Was n't that mortgage " good debt " ? @@120444568 <h> In its pursuit of Instagrammable spectacle , the Yayoi Kusama retrospective at NGV International misses opportunities to draw visitors into her complexities . By Dee Jefferson . <h> Yayoi Kusama retrospective at NGV International <p> Around the age of 10 , Yayoi Kusama started experiencing hallucinations . The first time it happened , she was sitting in a field of violets at her family 's seed-harvesting farm in the regional Japanese city of Matsumoto . She looked up and saw that every violet had a human-like facial expression and was talking to her -- loudly . " I was so terrified that my legs began shaking , " she writes in her biography . Another time , after studying a pattern of red flowers on a tablecloth , she saw the same red flowers plastered all over her own body and every surface around her . " In that instant my soul was obliterated and I was restored , returned to infinity , to eternal time and absolute space , " she writes . Again , it was a distressing experience : " My body was caught in that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , has said that these visions and their attendant psychological angst -- the byproduct of " obsessional neurosis " -- have fuelled her art-making : she describes herself as a " slave to creation " , compelled to disgorge her imaginative wellspring . For a viewer , Kusama 's hallucinations unlock a layer of meaning within a body of work known for its " infinity " patterns of dots , flowers and pumpkins . They make works such as her obliteration rooms -- in which she invites audience members to cover fully furnished rooms in stickers of colourful dots or flowers -- seem less facile and more poetic . The hallucinations also go some way to explaining Kusama 's retreat to a psychiatric hospital in Japan in 1977 , where she still lives and works , and her consistently obsessive arts practice across the decades . <p> So it 's surprising to see this key biographical detail mentioned only perfunctorily in the introductory wall text for NGV International 's juggernaut survey of Kusama 's career , although it pops up at the end as an afterthought . Spanning eight decades @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mid-career sculpture and video , and her Insta-famous mirrored " infinity rooms " -- Yayoi Kusama purports to be a definitive exhibition of the celebrated artist . <p> Kusama is a titan , generating massive audiences and auction prices ... But for all her fame and visual dominance , relatively little is known about the artist herself . <p> It 's a worthy project : by almost every metric Kusama is a titan , generating massive audiences and auction prices and commercial collaborations with the likes of Louis Vuitton . But for all her fame and visual dominance , relatively little is known about the artist herself . Most people know her only as the " one who does dots " . Many self-professed art lovers would have encountered her infinity rooms and pumpkin sculptures -- on social media at the very least -- and perhaps even know that she wears a bright red wig and lives in a mental hospital . Few can tell you much more . <p> NGV 's curators approach the task of elucidating this enigmatic figure chronologically , across two parts . The first charts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ New York in 1957 , aged 28 , and the frenetic 15 years of art-making that followed , taking in her experiments in minimalism , pop art , performance art and " happenings " , and forms as diverse as sculpture , collage , video and fashion . <p> In the exhibition 's second half , across the other side of the gallery 's forecourt , visitors encounter Kusama 's pumpkin-related paintings and sculptures , which emerged in the 1970s after her return to Japan , the large-scale flower sculptures and monumental and multi-panel paintings of the ' 80s and ' 90s , and her immersive room installations from the past three decades . The NGV exhibition boasts 10 of these -- the most ever assembled in one place -- including three of the infinity rooms for which Kusama is best known ( her most recent , 2024 's Infinity Mirrored Room -- My Heart is Filled to the Brim with Sparkling Light , has its world premiere in the exhibition ) . <p> Few exhibits have caused the frenzy that Kusama 's infinity rooms have : across the globe @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ less in these mirror-lined boxes , whose brightly coloured landscapes of tentacles , pumpkins and spheres and mesmerising lighting displays guarantee eye-catching , Insta-friendly selfies . Most audiences encounter them in this way : as commodified spectacle . It 's doubtful many engage -- or are afforded the time to engage -- with Kusama 's more spiritual invitation : to consider yourself as a mere speck within the infinite . Either way , the infinity rooms are a sensory sugar hit that 's hard to resist . You could do worse than send people with no knowledge of Kusama 's work to the second half of the exhibition first , to be dazzled -- and then back to the beginning , to understand how she got there and what it all means . <p> For anyone who has already encountered Kusama 's pumpkins and mirror boxes , the more thrilling material is in the exhibition 's first half . This opens with a darkened antechamber featuring psychologically charged drawings and paintings from her early years . <p> Born in 1929 , the youngest of four , Kusama grew up in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ social conservatism and what she has described as " a toxic family mix " . Her father , who had relinquished his name when he married into the wealthy Kusama family , repaid that humiliation by womanising . Her mother , who the artist describes as having a " hair-trigger temper " , tasked her youngest daughter with surveilling and reporting on him . When Kusama failed , she was beaten . Her art-making similarly enraged her mother : artists and actors were " disreputable at best " . Against this unhappy backdrop -- and fuelled by hallucinations -- Kusama churned out reams of drawings and then paintings , using whatever materials she could get hold of . <p> Kusama 's early works are among the most astonishing in an exhibition that 's not short on surprises . A double-sided drawing made at the age of 10 shows a vase of flowers on one side , enmeshed in a web of lines and dots , and a rudimentary sketch of a kimono-clad woman thought to be her mother on the other , also superimposed with a pattern of dots . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ eerie . The most startling work is a surrealist landscape painted when Kusama was 21 , depicting a fleshy vortex -- ridged , as if inside the guts or gullet -- narrowing to an aperture in which two skeletal trees are seen as if at a great distance . The title -- Accumulation of the Corpses ( Prisoner Surrounded by the Curtain of Depersonalization ) -- refers to what Kusama describes in her biography as a " silk-like curtain of indeterminate grey " that descended between her and her surroundings frequently during childhood , rendering other people tiny as if far away , and robbing her of her sense of time and speed , and her ability to converse . She writes of feeling imprisoned in this state -- hence the claustrophobia of the painting . <p> The omission of this context from the artwork 's label feels like a missed opportunity -- one of several in the exhibition 's opening stretch . Likewise , Kusama 's fear of sex and aversion to genitalia , which stems from her childhood environment and experiences , is not addressed . It leaves @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ works such as her Accumulations sculptures ( featuring soft silver protuberances on furniture and household items ) and 1965 's Infinity Mirror Room -- Phalli 's Field ( or Floor Show ) , featuring polka-dotted red and white phallus-like forms . There are counterproductive narrative omissions elsewhere , including the flummoxing failure to mention Kusama 's close personal and artistic relationship with American assemblage artist Joseph Cornell , which was instrumental in her creation of collage and diorama works featured in the exhibition . <p> And there are missed opportunities for connection : Kusama 's Self-Obliteration , a hypnotic psychedelic film from 1967 , is placed in a thoroughfare next to a fashion exhibit , where visitors will find it almost impossible to stop for the video 's 23-minute duration . This positioning suggests the film is more of a curio : in fact it 's a fascinating amalgam of Kusama 's art , biography and psychology up to that point in time , suggesting the ways in which it interconnects , and lending resonance to many of the works in the exhibition . <p> The more pernicious design flaw @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to a chronological narrative : having navigated the gargantuan field of work , visitors find themselves running a gauntlet of immersive rooms . Nothing dampens wonder quite like being herded through one infinity room after another in groups of eight to 12 , for 30 seconds a pop . Hot tip : skip the razzle-dazzle rooms and use the time to savour the more esoteric , weird and wonderful fruits of Kusamania . <p> Yayoi Kusama is showing at NGV International , Melbourne , until April 21 . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on January 25 , 2025 as " Joining the dots " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@120444570 <h> Sean Wilson You Must Remember This <p> The literature of dementia is not large . There are nonfictional exceptions , such as Annie Ernaux 's wrenching account of her mother 's descent into Alzheimer 's , I Remain in Darkness , Wendy Mitchell 's deeply moving memoir of early-onset dementia , Somebody I Used to Know , and novels and stories such as Lisa Genova 's Still Alice , Fiona McFarlane 's The Night Guest and Alice Munro 's remarkable " The Bear Came Over the Mountain " . But the subject remains relatively unexamined in either memoir or fiction . <p> It is n't difficult to guess why this is the case . Dementia 's invisibility in literature is just one aspect of our culture 's larger unease with ageing and death . The condition presents narrative , methodological and ethical challenges because those who experience it are often unable to describe it from within , and the lives of the old are not often accorded the level of concern that attaches to other phases of life . <p> Sean Wilson 's brief but beautifully wrought sophomore novel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to this body of writing . Centring on Grace , a woman in later life who is slowly unravelling as her memory fades , it captures not just the confusion and grief of that process but also the ways in which it robs those afflicted with it of agency over their own lives . <p> The action of the novel is , perhaps unsurprisingly , relatively confined . Grace , a widow , initially " fine , most of the time " , becomes unable to care for herself . She is shifted into aged care , where her condition gradually worsens , leaving her increasingly uncertain where she is and eventually unable to recognise her daughter and granddaughter . As Grace 's ability to make sense of her present decreases , her past begins to intrude in new and unpredictable ways , bringing back memories not just of her adult life but also her childhood and adolescence , and her difficult relationship with her alcoholic mother and gambler father . <p> Wilson 's writing is lucid and often extremely beautiful in its precision -- early on he describes Grace @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , when she can carry both the past and present in her mind , unbroken like a stitch along a hem " -- which sharpens the emotional impact of Grace 's decline . Simultaneously the novel captures how days and weeks blur into one another by jumbling the chronology of the novel , so it begins with chapter 10 , before shifting to chapters 7 , 11 , 12 , 8 and so on . <p> As this temporal slippage intensifies , Grace 's life begins to dissolve into a kaleidoscope of vividly rendered memories and moments of confusion closer to the present , out of which various figures emerge . One of these figures is her daughter , Liz , a lawyer , who works in " the Magistrates Court -- or is it the County Court ? Grace ca n't remember which it is , but they are all the same ... leather briefcases , stern faces , shuffling papers . The occasional television crew waiting outside . " Although Liz is responsible for Grace 's care , she is -- clearly deliberately -- a relatively fugitive presence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gradually assumes control over her mother 's life . <p> Interestingly this does not make the sections involving Liz any less affecting . Instead it allows them to speak powerfully to the challenges of caring for the aged . In Liz 's brief appearances one glimpses her struggles to balance the troubles of her own life -- the husband who leaves her , her conflicts with her teenage daughter -- with her mother 's needs . <p> It also offers a tacit reminder of just how gendered the division of emotional and physical labour of caring for the elderly is , a reality that is perhaps also visible in the fact that the vast bulk of both memoirs and novels about dementia are written by and about women . <p> Grace 's husband , Harold , is also seen only glancingly , flitting in and out as little more than a memory of love and stability . Indeed , Grace 's life with him often seems little more than a temporary refuge from the chaos of her upbringing . <p> Significantly it is those early years that loom largest as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's upbringing , Wilson writes perceptively about the effects of addiction upon children , capturing the way alcohol " was always there , in someone 's hand , ice bobbing on the surface , condensation beading on the glass " , and her mother 's narcissism and unpredictable oscillations between affection and anger . The novel also drives home her parents ' negligence , and how their behaviour forces the young Grace to assume responsibility not just for her younger siblings but also her parents , and the damage that inflicts . <p> You Must Remember This is also quietly but inescapably political , exploring the ways in which the old and infirm are robbed of agency and infantilised . While we are reminded several times that the aged-care home Grace finds herself in is one of the better ones , it is still not a place anybody would choose to be . <p> The real achievement of Wilson 's novel is its desire to give shape to the experience of dementia , and what it must be like to try to hold on to one 's sense of self @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , midway through the book , " some days , yesterday is like those paintings she saw in a gallery she visited with Liz years ago . Big canvases with splashes of colour moving in all directions . No order : chaos . On those days , her memory is a room filled with these paintings and she can get no meaning from them . On those days , she is standing in the centre of the room , spinning around and around , searching the canvases for meaning , trying to get some sense of order in the paint , some sense of what the story is and where she fits . Its origins go back at least to the 15th century in Britain . Over the centuries , it has been made smoother and is now a semi-set cream , flavoured with lemon . The cream is no longer split -- the acid is used just to set it . <p> I find posset is great for the time-poor who are thinking ahead . C. <p> Cut the apricots in half and remove the stones , then place a tablespoon of the flavoured butter on each @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ paper . <p> Bake in the oven for 10 to 15 minutes until they start to colour and caramelise , then sprinkle with the extra tablespoon of sugar and continue to cook for another five minutes until they are nicely caramelised . Our terms and conditions of membership still apply . <h> When it comes to Australia Day , wattle stop the arguments ? <h> At this time of year , we 're reminded that Australia has a problem : an ongoing and deeply divisive conflict over Australia Day . For many , January 26 is a joyous celebration of national pride ; a day of barbecues , citizenship ceremonies , and fireworks . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ flags fluttering under the summer sun . But for others , especially for Indigenous Australians , it is a day of mourning , marking the beginning of dispossession , violence , and generational trauma . Far from fostering national unity , Australia Day has become a battleground of contested memory and competing narratives . The debate intensifies each year , spilling into heated discussions about identity , history , and politics . What should be a moment of shared celebration now serves as a reminder of the unresolved tensions at the heart of Australia 's story . Resolving this division is critical for national harmony , but how can we find a path forward ? <p> At the heart of this conflict lies the weight of history . For Aboriginal Australians , January 26 is ' Invasion Day , ' ' Survival Day , ' or a ' Day of Mourning , ' as it marks the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788 . It signals the beginning of colonisation , a process that led to the dispossession of land , the dismantling of cultures , and the marginalisation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and its effects are felt today . The socioeconomic disparities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians are stark : reduced life expectancy , chronic health issues , lower educational attainment , and higher rates of incarceration . The intergenerational trauma of the Stolen Generations remains unresolved . <p> For some non-Indigenous Australians , however , January 26 represents a celebration of their nation 's achievements and identity , a day to reflect on progress , multiculturalism , and shared values . Many view the date as symbolic of belonging and continuity , a fixed point in the calendar that anchors them to the nation 's story . <p> This tension between the celebration of progress and the mourning of dispossession fuels the Australia Day debate . Calls to ' change the date ' are met with resistance , often framed as attacks on tradition . Social media amplifies these clashes , with some Australians dismissing Indigenous concerns as ' political correctness ' or ' wokeism . ' Comments like ' 1788 was a long time ago just get over it ' ignore the enduring scars of colonization , which do not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has been further inflamed by political opportunism . Australia Day has become a symbolic battleground where right-wing populists have attempted to exploit national pride and cultural nostalgia . We 've seen Peter Dutton adopt a populist weaponising of identity politics as a substitute for policy questions around issues like the Voice , flags , and now Australia Day . He has framed the national day controversy as a struggle between ' ordinary Australians ' and an out-of-touch elite , painting critics of January 26 as enemies of tradition . Dutton finds his ammunition among two groups : older generations who rightly want to celebrate the best aspects of our story and immigrant generations ( the main groups at Australia Day parades ) who want to show the most reasonable gratitude for what Australia has given them . <p> This rhetoric resonates with many Australians who feel alienated by rapid societal change . By caricaturing progressives as ' elites ' and Indigenous advocates as ' divisive , ' populists reduce the complexities of the issue to a binary conflict . The result is a cultural war of ' us versus them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ flattened into slogans and soundbites . <p> Media outlets like those of the Murdoch press amplify these divisions , presenting any critique of Australia Day as an attack on the nation itself . Yet this approach overlooks the fundamental problem : January 26 is not a date that unifies , it divides . The refusal to address the historical and emotional weight of the day only deepens the rift . <h> ' Such a change would , of course , not come overnight . Building a new tradition takes time and commitment . But the rewards of a national day that unites rather than divides are well worth the effort . ' <p> Somewhat ironically , the symbolic significance of January 26 is a relatively recent construct . Originally known as Sydney Anniversary Day , the occasion was a local celebration commemorating eight days after the First Fleet 's arrival at Botany Bay . For much of its history , the date was a modest affair , recognized formally in 1935 but observed without much fanfare . <p> It was n't until the 1990s that Australia Day became a major @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and a concerted push for patriotic celebration elevated its status . In 1994 , Jeff Kennett spearheaded efforts to fix the public holiday to January 26 , cementing its place in the calendar . <p> This transformation , however , came at a cost . What was once a relaxed , inclusive occasion has become a flashpoint for division . The competing narratives around Australia Day , one of celebration and the other of mourning , underscore the difficulty of using a single date to encapsulate a complex national story . <p> In a surprising about-turn , in 2019 , Jeff Kennett described Australia Day on 26 January as ' a joke ' and ' lacking credibility ' , suggesting a move to the first of January . We now have a deeply entrenched politicized rhetorical civil war over Australia Day on 26 January . It will not go away . <p> As the Australia Day debate reaches an impasse , it is clear that neither clinging to January 26 nor ignoring the controversy will resolve the issue . What is needed is a new approach , a national day @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ modern Australia . <p> One potential solution lies in Wattle Day , celebrated on September 1 . Rooted in nature , the wattle is a symbol of resilience , renewal , and shared heritage . Unlike January 26 , it carries no historical baggage , offering a fresh start for an inclusive celebration . <p> Traditions can evolve . Just as Canada embraced the maple leaf as a national emblem , Australia can adopt the golden wattle as a unifying symbol . Wattle Day could begin modestly , with schools , councils , and community groups celebrating the day in parks and public spaces . Over time , it could grow into a public holiday that honours the land , its people , and their shared future . <p> This shift would not erase history but acknowledge it . Wattle Day could complement other moments of reflection , such as NAIDOC Week , ensuring that the stories of First Nations peoples remain central to the national narrative . <p> A Wattle Day holiday would also offer practical benefits . Falling after three months of winter without public holidays , most @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a welcome respite before the busy spring season . Citizenship ceremonies could feature sprigs of wattle , symbolising unity and renewal . <p> A Wattle Day national holiday would be enjoyed by all Australians . Eventually , it would put aside the annual symbolic conflicts which now mars every January . And over time , Wattle Day could inspire broader cultural shifts , perhaps even a new national flag featuring a bright yellow wattle against a green background or against a blue sky . <p> Such a change would , of course , not come overnight . Building a new tradition takes time and commitment . But the rewards of a national day that unites rather than divides are well worth the effort . <p> Ultimately the Australia Day debate will not resolve itself . Continuing to celebrate on January 26 guarantees further division , deepening the fractures in Australia 's national identity . Embracing Wattle Day as a new national holiday offers a possible way forward , a chance to leave behind the pain and controversy of the past and build a more inclusive , harmonious future . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ time to let this unifying symbol take root . A Wattle Day Australia Day could become a celebration for all Australians , offering hope , healing , and a shared vision for the years ahead . <h> Dr. Stephen Alomes of RMIT University is an historian of Australian nationalism and a painter of wattles . <h> SUPPORT RESPECTFUL CONVERSATIONS IN A TIME OF DIVISION <p> We need no reminding of the depth of the division that exists in our Australian community . It 's there every time we go online , turn on the TV , open the newspaper . <p> Our politics is focused on point-scoring , personalities , and name-calling across party lines . The media , for the most part , do n't help , driven by the 24-hour news cycle and the pursuit of advertising dollars into a frenzy of click-bait and shallow sensationalism . <p> What does it mean to be an Australian in times like these ? Make sure the installer you 're signing on with will be the one to do the work . <p> " There are a lot of high-pressure marketing companies out there that are sort of posing as solar companies , " Gold-Markel said . " <p> Make sure you know who 's actually going to be doing the work of putting solar panels on your house before you sign on the dotted line . <p> Sandy Huffaker/Bloomberg via Getty Images <h> 8 . What 's your timeline for installation ? <p> You 'll want to discuss a rough @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ both in terms of when work will begin and how long it will take to get your solar installation up and running . Hale noted that 's a question a reputable installer should be asking you . <p> " Installers should ask what your timeframe is for getting your system installed , so they can give you the room to do your research , " she said . " The really good installers will wait for you to come back to them . " <h> 9 . What kinds of maintenance packages or warranties are available ? <p> Gold-Markel recommends inquiring about extended warranties or operations and maintenance packages that cover the entire life of the system , which is typically around 25 years . " Ask if you can also get an operations and maintenance package , an extended warranty that covers the lifespan of the solar or a longer warranty for the workmanship than may come with the contract , " he said . <p> Due to high interest rates , financing your solar installation is a less attractive option than it was a few years ago . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sure to inquire about any hidden fees that may be a part of the agreement . It 's also important to look into the institution offering the loan , which may be a third party , and read the terms closely to understand what happens if you default . <h> 11 . What is the cost of my solar system in dollars per watt ? <p> Homeowners tend to focus on the total cost to install solar or the cost per panel . Be sure to compare the cost in dollars per watt when comparing solar installers , Hale said . Two solar systems may have a similar overall cost , but the wattage generated can differ based on panel size and capacity . The system with the lower cost per watt is the better deal . <h> 12 . How much consumption is my solar energy going to offset ? <p> A good solar installer should make it easy to understand how much of your household 's power consumption can be met by your solar system . Factors like weather , shade , roof size and household energy use @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Information about how much of your household 's electricity will be offset by your system should be included in a reputable solar installer 's proposal for your project , and installers should be forthcoming about this information . " If that 's clearly laid out in a proposal , then nine times out of ten , that 's a green flag , " Hale said . <h> 13 . What are the lifetime savings based on ? <p> Your discussions with solar installers should not only estimate how much you 'll save over the life of your system but also include how that estimate was derived . <p> Installers calculate lifetime savings using a metric called a utility escalator . This percentage describes the projected inflation rate of the cost of power and is based on historical trends ( and is different from the escalators in a power purchase agreement ) . Solar United Neighbors recommends checking that the utility escalator used in competing proposals from different installers is the same to help you compare accurately . <h> 14 . Is the power generation estimate guaranteed ? <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ your solar system will always produce power at the maximum level , said Gold-Markel , but a good installer should be able to guarantee your panels ' performance within a reasonable range . <p> " If the overall power output is within a reasonable error rate of , say , 10% of what was predicted , then I think you should be happy with the outcome , " he says . <h> 15 . How do I sell solar energy credits back to the grid ? <p> Net metering policies in some states allow you to sell power generated by your solar system back to the public grid -- a significant solar incentive that can significantly reduce the payback period on your system . You do n't typically sell that power to your energy utility directly . <p> Instead , homeowners often sell solar renewable energy certificates , or SRECs , through a third party known as a broker or aggregator . Your installer may be able to connect you with a broker . If you 'd prefer to choose your own broker , Solar United Neighbors recommends double-checking your @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agreement . <h> Our Experts <p> CNET staff -- not advertisers , partners or business interests -- determine how we review the products and services we cover . But as is often the case , it was n't that simple . <p> Sam Hawley : Yeah , because you 've actually found that while that was one case , the financial ombudsman is n't taking on lots and lots of others . <p> Michael Atkin : That 's right . So Mark Stacey , who I mentioned earlier , tried to take on his insurer over his 75% price rise . And it was only when he went to the ombudsman that the insurer actually gave him more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , they said it was due to doing a pricing review and finding that actually they had more increased costs due to natural disasters and increased claims costs . And the price of insurance for them had increased and the price of insuring his house had increased . But this year , they said it was a change in information about the bushfire risk . And that was the first time he said he 'd heard that information . Despite that , the ombudsman refused to take on his case . They found that he had not demonstrated that the premium was incorrectly applied . And this comes down to the ombudsman has really strict rules about whether you can take on your insurer over a premium increase . They can only consider if the premium 's been incorrectly calculated , whether there 's been some kind of non-disclosure or a breach of the law or some kind of misrepresentation . That 's frustrated people like Mark and consumer groups because they argue , well , the insurer does n't disclose how they calculate these premiums . @@120511791 <h> Trump is ditching climate action , again . This time , there are ways to fight back <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> When a triumphant Donald Trump reclaimed the White House last week , he wasted no time in declaring war . Not a trade war , nor an invasion of Greenland or Canada , but effectively a war on the environment . <p> US President Donald Trump signs a slew of executive orders on the first day of his presidency.Credit : AP <p> First , he signed an executive order to withdraw the United States from the United Nations climate treaty . The US is now only one of four countries not in the Paris Agreement -- the others are Iran , Libya and Yemen . <p> He declared an " energy emergency " , with the aim of garnering increased powers to approve production of fossil fuels , particularly in Alaska . Though , in a bet each way , it will also cover critical green minerals . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ included a laundry list of actions -- declaring it official policy to encourage energy exploration of the continental shelf , eliminating a supposed electric vehicle mandate that apparently does not exist in law anyway , and safeguarding the right of Americans to choose their own lightbulbs . <p> By delivering all this within hours of the inauguration , Trump signalled his intention to do everything within his power to expand fossil fuels or " drill , baby , drill " . <p> The question is : how much power does he have ? Within the US , quite a lot , given Republicans control Congress and the conservative majority on the Supreme Court . However , much of the real work to reduce greenhouse emissions in the US is actually happening at state level and that will continue . <p> Advertisement <p> The bigger question is how much influence Trump has outside the US . This is up to us . There is a world where Trump 's actions mean the global race to decarbonise loses momentum . <p> Economics describes " the free rider problem " , where some @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a fair share ( or paying nothing at all ) for a shared resource . If the world 's largest economy is free riding by not cutting emissions , the other Paris signatories may be less inclined to do their part as well . <p> Australia is a small contributor to global emissions -- if you do n't count our fossil fuel exports -- but we ca n't afford to get left behind . <p> Pessimism about our collective ability to effectively tackle climate change can also mean people -- voters , business leaders and politicians -- succumb to despair . This can lead to a nihilistic impulse -- the attitude that " the world is burning , so I may as well look after No.1 " . <p> Finally , politicians who seek to emulate Trump and exploit mistrust of renewables may gain the ascendancy . There are certainly signs this could happen in Australia . Yet , there is also a world where other countries go hell for leather in cutting emissions while waiting for the US to return to the fold . <p> Do n't forget , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ US from global climate treaties the first time he was president . Global investors will be looking to redirect that money , and Australia has a chance to capitalise on this situation , or it will cede ground to other countries . <p> As one example , the Danish owner of Star of the South in Gippsland is looking at possible new sites for offshore wind projects including in Australia and New Zealand . <p> Many large countries and groupings have finally hit their stride with decarbonisation and this wo n't be abandoned just because of Trump . <p> In the European Union , Carbon Brief reports that coal power use has fallen by almost two-thirds in the past decade , while solar @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ coal generation for the first time ; and wind power has doubled . <p> Loading <p> And what about the world 's largest emitter of carbon dioxide ? China installed a massive 301 gigawatts of renewable capacity including solar , wind and hydro in 2023 alone , more than the total renewable generating capacity installed in most countries over all time . As of May 2024 , " clean energy " generated a record high 44 per cent of China 's electricity . <p> Will Europe and China simply let the US be a free rider ? They have plenty of ways to fight back . <p> Europe is phasing in a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism , a fee or tariff levied on imported goods based on the greenhouse gases emitted during their production . It is due to be fully operational by 2026 . <p> China , while critical of the European levy as protectionism in a green guise , is no stranger to a surgically targeted tariff . What the superpower does in response to Trump walking back climate policies remains to be seen . <p> Australia has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Border Adjustment Mechanism . <p> Australian export businesses need to be ready for this new development .
